Read these four local documents in full and report what they mandate:

- /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann_frontend_lead_playbook.md
- /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/uiBuild-knowledge.md
- /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/fedBuild-manual.md
- /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/fedLead-playbook.md

For EACH file report:
1. Its stated purpose, and any header/frontmatter indicating status (live, draft, ARCHIVED, superseded, deprecated) and last-updated date.
2. Concrete, actionable rules it lays down for building UI components — component structure, styling approach, theme recipes, tokens, testing expectations, naming, folder layout, story requirements, definition-of-done.
3. Anything it says about workflow, process, or how work should be sequenced/reviewed.

Then answer these specific questions:
- Which of the four, if any, is archived or superseded? Be explicit — quote the marker.
- Do any of them CONFLICT with each other? Quote both sides.
- Do any of them conflict with the repo's own rules in /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/rules/*.md (particularly overrideStyling.md, components.md, css.md, testing.md)? Quote both sides where they differ.

Be precise and quote directly. Give file:line references. Do not summarise vaguely — I need the actual mandated rules, verbatim where they matter. Report back in a structured form; do not edit anything.

- playwright-skill: Complete browser automation with Playwright. Auto-detects dev servers, writes clean test scripts to /tmp. Test pages, fill forms, take screenshots, check responsive design, validate UX, test login flows, check links, automate any browser task. Use when user wants to test websites, automate browser interactions, validate web functionality, or perform any browser-based testing.
- audit-tier: Identify the protection tier, owner, and import blast radius of a file or directory under overrides/. Use before editing anything you're unsure about.
- code-quality: Audit recently changed or specified files for code quality issues — naming, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence, and structural debt. Read-only. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR.
- code-review: AI-powered code review using CodeRabbit. Default code-review skill. Trigger for any explicit review request AND autonomously when the agent thinks a review is needed (code/PR/quality/security).
- contentful-register-component: Register a Zimmermann React component with Contentful Studio Experiences. Use when a developer asks to register, add, or expose a React component to Contentful, or when they need to create a Contentful component definition for an existing component.
- feature-spec: Turn a plain-English feature request into a scoped implementation plan before any code is written. Asks one clarifying question at a time, then produces a spec Claude Code can execute safely. Use this before starting any non-trivial implementation session.
- generate-changelog: Generate a release changelog from conventional commits and upstream baseline notes. Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release. Use before cutting a release branch or when preparing release notes.
- new-component: Scaffold a new Zimmermann component under overrides/app/components/ — TypeScript, Chakra-first, with a paired Storybook story. Use whenever a new custom component is needed.
- onboarding: Interactive onboarding for new developers and QA engineers joining the Zimmermann PWA Kit project. Asks role at the start, checks the mechanical setup items, then orients the person to the rules and tools relevant to their role and squad. Run this in the first Claude Code session on a new machine or a first day on the project.
- pr-checklist: Generate a PR description and merge checklist based on the files changed on the current branch. Pairs with /code-quality.
- project-init: One-time project setup walkthrough. Runs the state detection script, fixes automatable items, asks one question at a time for human-input items, and updates the 7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist Confluence page as each item is confirmed. Run this once when setting up the project for the first time, or when returning to check setup status.
- qa-generate: Generate a Gherkin .feature file and Playwright test spec from a Jira story. Human-in-the-lead — Lead QA validates the .feature before Playwright is generated. Use for any new storefront user journey that needs E2E test coverage.
- scope-check: Review a proposed Claude Code prompt for scope safety before it runs. Classifies every likely-touched file by tier and verdicts the prompt SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED, rewriting it when needed.
- session-start: Run the mandatory session start ritual — reads tracking docs, runs branch + health checks, states current position. Use at the start of every coding session.
- upstream-sync-review: Review the release notes / changelog for a new @salesforce/retail-react-app version before bumping. Lightweight policy — see .docs/upstreamPolicy.md.
- code-review:code-review: Code review a pull request
- feature-dev:feature-dev: Guided feature development with codebase understanding and architecture focus
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- commit-commands:clean_gone: Cleans up all git branches marked as [gone] (branches that have been deleted on the remote but still exist locally), including removing associated worktrees.
- commit-commands:commit-push-pr: Commit, push, and open a PR
- commit-commands:commit: Create a git commit
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- pr-review-toolkit:review-pr: Comprehensive PR review using specialized agents
- agent-sdk-dev:new-sdk-app: Create and setup a new Claude Agent SDK application
- plugin-dev:create-plugin: Guided end-to-end plugin creation workflow with component design, implementation, and validation
- vercel:bootstrap: Bootstrap a repository with Vercel-linked resources by running preflight checks, provisioning integrations, verifying env keys, and then executing db/dev startup commands safely.
- vercel:deploy: Deploy the current project to Vercel. Pass "prod" or "production" as argument to deploy to production. Default is preview deployment.
- vercel:env: Manage Vercel environment variables. Commands include list, pull, add, remove, and diff. Use to sync environment variables between Vercel and your local development environment.
- vercel:status: Show the status of the current Vercel project — recent deployments, linked project info, and environment overview.
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- superpowers:brainstorming: You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation.
- superpowers:dispatching-parallel-agents: Use when facing 2+ independent tasks that can be worked on without shared state or sequential dependencies
- superpowers:executing-plans: Use when you have a written implementation plan to execute in a separate session with review checkpoints
- superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch: Use when implementation is complete, all tests pass, and you need to decide how to integrate the work
- superpowers:receiving-code-review: Use when receiving code review feedback, before implementing suggestions, especially if feedback seems unclear or technically questionable - requires technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement or blind implementation
- superpowers:requesting-code-review: Use when completing tasks, implementing major features, or before merging to verify work meets requirements
- superpowers:subagent-driven-development: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session
- superpowers:systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
- superpowers:test-driven-development: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code
- superpowers:using-git-worktrees: Use when starting feature work that needs isolation from current workspace or before executing implementation plans - ensures an isolated workspace exists via native tools or git worktree fallback
- superpowers:using-superpowers: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions
- superpowers:verification-before-completion: Use when about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing, before committing or creating PRs - requires running verification commands and confirming output before making any success claims; evidence before assertions always
- superpowers:writing-plans: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code
- superpowers:writing-skills: Use when creating new skills, editing existing skills, or verifying skills work before deployment
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.
- figma:figma-use: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `use_figma` tool call. NEVER call `use_figma` directly without loading this skill first. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.
- figma:figma-use-figjam: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the FigJam context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- figma:figma-use-motion: Motion / animation context for the `use_figma` MCP tool — animating Figma nodes via manual keyframes, animation styles, easing, and timeline duration. Load alongside figma-use whenever a task involves adding, editing, or inspecting animation on a node.
- figma:figma-use-slides: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the Slides context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- claude-code-setup:claude-automation-recommender: Analyze a codebase and recommend Claude Code automations (hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, MCP servers). Use when user asks for automation recommendations, wants to optimize their Claude Code setup, mentions improving Claude Code workflows, asks how to first set up Claude Code for a project, or wants to know what Claude Code features they should use.
- plugin-dev:agent-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create an agent", "add an agent", "write a subagent", "agent frontmatter", "when to use description", "agent examples", "agent tools", "agent colors", "autonomous agent", or needs guidance on agent structure, system prompts, triggering conditions, or agent development best practices for Claude Code plugins.
- plugin-dev:command-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a slash command", "add a command", "write a custom command", "define command arguments", "use command frontmatter", "organize commands", "create command with file references", "interactive command", "use AskUserQuestion in command", or needs guidance on slash command structure, YAML frontmatter fields, dynamic arguments, bash execution in commands, user interaction patterns, or command development best practices for Claude Code.
- plugin-dev:hook-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a hook", "add a PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop hook", "validate tool use", "implement prompt-based hooks", "use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}", "set up event-driven automation", "block dangerous commands", or mentions hook events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SubagentStop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, PreCompact, Notification). Provides comprehensive guidance for creating and implementing Claude Code plugin hooks with focus on advanced prompt-based hooks API.
- plugin-dev:mcp-integration: This skill should be used when the user asks to "add MCP server", "integrate MCP", "configure MCP in plugin", "use .mcp.json", "set up Model Context Protocol", "connect external service", mentions "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} with MCP", or discusses MCP server types (SSE, stdio, HTTP, WebSocket). Provides comprehensive guidance for integrating Model Context Protocol servers into Claude Code plugins for external tool and service integration.
- plugin-dev:plugin-settings: This skill should be used when the user asks about "plugin settings", "store plugin configuration", "user-configurable plugin", ".local.md files", "plugin state files", "read YAML frontmatter", "per-project plugin settings", or wants to make plugin behavior configurable. Documents the .claude/plugin-name.local.md pattern for storing plugin-specific configuration with YAML frontmatter and markdown content.
- plugin-dev:plugin-structure: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a plugin", "scaffold a plugin", "understand plugin structure", "organize plugin components", "set up plugin.json", "use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}", "add commands/agents/skills/hooks", "configure auto-discovery", or needs guidance on plugin directory layout, manifest configuration, component organization, file naming conventions, or Claude Code plugin architecture best practices.
- plugin-dev:skill-development: This skill should be used when the user wants to "create a skill", "add a skill to plugin", "write a new skill", "improve skill description", "organize skill content", or needs guidance on skill structure, progressive disclosure, or skill development best practices for Claude Code plugins.
- vercel:ai-gateway: Vercel AI Gateway expert guidance. Use when configuring model routing, provider failover, cost tracking, or managing multiple AI providers through a unified API.
- vercel:ai-sdk: Vercel AI SDK expert guidance. Use when building AI-powered features — chat interfaces, text generation, structured output, tool calling, agents, MCP integration, streaming, embeddings, reranking, image generation, or working with any LLM provider.
- vercel:auth: Authentication integration guidance — Clerk (native Vercel Marketplace), Descope, and Auth0 setup for Next.js applications. Covers middleware auth patterns, sign-in/sign-up flows, and Marketplace provisioning. Use when implementing user authentication.
- vercel:cdn-caching: Debug Vercel CDN caching — cache hit rate, stale content, revalidation behavior, ISR + PPR, per-request cache reasons (cacheReason), and costs.
- vercel:chat-sdk: Vercel Chat SDK expert guidance. Use when building multi-platform chat bots — Slack, Telegram, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Google Chat, GitHub, Linear — with a single codebase. Covers the Chat class, adapters, threads, messages, cards, modals, streaming, state management, and webhook setup.
- vercel:deployments-cicd: Vercel deployment and CI/CD expert guidance. Use when deploying, promoting, rolling back, inspecting deployments, building with --prebuilt, or configuring CI workflow files for Vercel.
- vercel:env-vars: Vercel environment variable expert guidance. Use when working with .env files, vercel env commands, OIDC tokens, or managing environment-specific configuration.
- vercel:eve: Build durable AI agents and agent-powered applications with the eve framework. Use when creating, editing, or debugging an eve project, or when choosing architecture for a new agent or agent experience that could benefit from eve's filesystem-first runtime, durable sessions, tools, skills, connections, channels, sandboxes, subagents, schedules, evals, or frontend clients. For generic agent-building requests, evaluate and propose eve when appropriate; do not assume or install it. Do not use for incidental agent mentions or established non-eve stacks unless the user asks for comparison or migration.
- vercel:knowledge-update: Corrects outdated LLM knowledge about the Vercel platform and introduces new products. Injected at session start.
- vercel:marketplace: Vercel Marketplace expert guidance — discovering, installing, and managing third-party integrations via the `vercel integration` CLI. Use when building any app that needs an external capability without a dedicated skill — commerce (stores, storefronts, selling products), payments (checkout, subscriptions, billing), observability/monitoring, messaging/email, search, or CMS — or when discovering, installing, or managing integrations.
- vercel:microfrontends: Guide for building, configuring, and deploying microfrontends on Vercel. Use this skill when the user mentions microfrontends, multi-zones, splitting an app across teams, independent deployments, cross-app routing, incremental migration, composing multiple frontends under one domain, microfrontends.json, @vercel/microfrontends, the microfrontends local proxy, or path-based routing between Vercel projects. Also use when the user asks about shared layouts across projects, navigation between microfrontends, fallback environments, asset prefixes, or feature flag controlled routing.
- vercel:next-cache-components: Next.js 16 Cache Components guidance — PPR, use cache directive, cacheLife, cacheTag, updateTag, and migration from unstable_cache. Use when implementing partial prerendering, caching strategies, or migrating from older Next.js cache patterns.
- vercel:next-forge: next-forge expert guidance — production-grade Turborepo monorepo SaaS starter by Vercel. Use when working in a next-forge project, scaffolding with `npx next-forge init`, or editing @repo/* workspace packages.
- vercel:next-upgrade: Upgrade Next.js to the latest version following official migration guides and codemods. Use when upgrading Next.js versions, running codemods, or migrating between major releases.
- vercel:nextjs: Next.js App Router expert guidance. Use when building, debugging, or architecting Next.js applications — routing, Server Components, Server Actions, Cache Components, layouts, middleware/proxy, data fetching, rendering strategies, and deployment on Vercel.
- vercel:react-best-practices: React best-practices reviewer for TSX files. Triggers after editing multiple TSX components to run a condensed quality checklist covering component structure, hooks usage, accessibility, performance, and TypeScript patterns.
- vercel:routing-middleware: Vercel Routing Middleware guidance — request interception before cache, rewrites, redirects, personalization. Works with any framework. Supports Edge, Node.js, and Bun runtimes. Use when intercepting requests at the platform level.
- vercel:runtime-cache: Vercel Runtime Cache API guidance — ephemeral per-region key-value cache with tag-based invalidation. Shared across Functions, Routing Middleware, and Builds. Use when implementing caching strategies beyond framework-level caching.
- vercel:shadcn: shadcn/ui expert guidance — CLI, component installation, composition patterns, custom registries, theming, Tailwind CSS integration, and high-quality interface design. Use when initializing shadcn, adding components, composing product UI, building custom registries, configuring themes, or troubleshooting component issues.
- vercel:turbopack: Turbopack expert guidance. Use when configuring the Next.js bundler, optimizing HMR, debugging build issues, or understanding the Turbopack vs Webpack differences.
- vercel:vercel-agent: Vercel Agent guidance — AI-powered code review, incident investigation, and SDK installation. Automates PR analysis and anomaly debugging. Use when configuring or understanding Vercel's AI development tools.
- vercel:vercel-cli: Vercel CLI expert guidance. Use when deploying, managing environment variables, linking projects, viewing logs, querying metrics, managing domains, or interacting with the Vercel platform from the command line.
- vercel:vercel-connect: Vercel Connect expert guidance — securely obtain scoped OAuth tokens for third-party services (Slack, GitHub, MCP servers, OAuth, Snowflake) on behalf of apps or users via Vercel OIDC. Use when wiring up third-party API access, connecting to MCP servers, sending Slack messages, accessing GitHub APIs, receiving webhook events from Slack/Linear/GitHub and forwarding them to your agents and apps, or building Eve agent connections.
- vercel:vercel-firewall: Vercel Firewall expert guidance — automatic DDoS mitigation, the Vercel WAF (custom rules, IP blocking, managed rulesets, rate limiting), Attack Mode, system bypass, bot management, and the `vercel firewall` CLI. Use when configuring platform-level security, responding to attacks, or staging firewall rules.
- vercel:vercel-functions: Vercel Functions expert guidance — Serverless Functions, Edge Functions, Fluid Compute, streaming, Cron Jobs, and runtime configuration. Use when configuring, debugging, or optimizing server-side code running on Vercel.
- vercel:vercel-sandbox
- vercel:vercel-storage: Vercel storage expert guidance — Blob, Edge Config, and Marketplace storage (Neon Postgres, Upstash Redis). Use when choosing, configuring, or using data storage with Vercel applications.
- vercel:verification
- vercel:workflow: Vercel Workflow DevKit (WDK) expert guidance. Use when building durable workflows, long-running tasks, API routes or agents that need pause/resume, retries, step-based execution, or crash-safe orchestration with Vercel Workflow.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	> # ⚠️ ARCHIVED — 25 August 2026
2	>
3	> **This document is retired and no longer maintained.** It was written 9 July 2026 from the
4	> Manila AI-engineering training week, whose vehicle was a Next.js / Tailwind / Contentful
5	> stack — not this project's Salesforce PWA Kit.
6	>
7	> **Its durable operating principles moved to `fedLead-playbook.md` §3 (Principles) and §4
8	> (Working with AI tooling).** The training-vehicle material was dropped rather than migrated:
9	> its artifacts (`build-log.md`, `component-registry.md`, the story skill) were training
10	> fixtures, and §16.1 of this document already conceded three of them were imagined.
11	>
12	> Kept on disk for provenance. Several claims below are contradicted by the current codebase —
13	> most notably that the generated registry "can't go stale" (its tier column is unreliable),
14	> that hardcoded hex values are mechanically checkable (they weren't until 23 Aug, and the
15	> script still isn't in CI), and that deployment parity is manual discipline (every branch now
16	> auto-deploys to its own MRT environment).
17	>
18	> **Do not cite this file.** Use `fedLead-playbook.md`, `fedBuild-manual.md`, or
19	> `uiBuild-knowledge.md`.
20	
21	---
22	
23	# The Frontend Development Lead Playbook
24	### Zimmermann Commerce Migration · How to be the FE Lead as both IC and Senior/Lead
25	
26	*Distilled from the Manila AI Engineering Training Week (June 2026, facilitated by Tim Lavelle). This is your operating manual, not a summary of the week.*
27	
28	---
29	
30	## 0. How to use this document
31	
32	This is the standard you hold yourself and your squad to. Read it once end-to-end, then treat it as a lookup — every section is written so you can jump to it mid-delivery.
33	
34	**Source and provenance — read this once so you never confuse the two layers:**
35	
36	- Everything in sections 1–9 is grounded in the **Manila training**. The training vehicle was a *TelcoNow B2C portal* on **Next.js 14 · TypeScript · Tailwind · Contentful**. That is what was actually taught.
37	- The training's *methodology* is deliberately stack-agnostic. Its closing thesis: **"The discipline transfers. The specific tools won't."** That is why it maps onto Zimmermann at all.
38	- Anything about **SFCC / PWA Kit / MRT / the two squads / RACI / CI-CD gates / integrations** is **me bridging to your project** from separate context (the solution deck and project setup). It is labeled as a bridge in **section 16**, which has since been verified against the real repo (2026-07-09) — corrections and open items are called out there, not silently folded in here. Don't cite section 16 as training content; it still isn't.
39	
40	**The three gaps you carry into this role — stated plainly, because pretending they aren't there is how leads fail:**
41	
42	1. **Framework gap.** You're Angular-primary. The training and the project are React (Next in training, PWA Kit in project). The *habits* below transfer cleanly. The *code idioms* do not. Build PWA Kit / React fluency as a separate, explicit track — don't let the transferable methodology fool you into thinking the framework transfers with it.
43	2. **Scale gap.** The training taught *solo* builds. You lead *shared-codebase, two-squad* delivery. Every "memory for future-you" artifact below has to be re-read as "contract for the whole team." Section 16 makes that jump concrete.
44	3. **Leadership gap.** You are stepping up into the lead seat. The IC craft you already have. The lead craft — running review culture, protecting quality under pressure, multiplying yourself — is the part this document is really for.
45	
46	---
47	
48	## 1. The one principle everything hangs on
49	
50	> **The quality ceiling is set by the human, not the AI.**
51	
52	Claude will match the quality of what you give it. Give it a vague plan, you get plausible garbage that costs hours to unwind. Give it a tight contract, sharp stories, and enforced rules, and you get output you'd have been proud to write yourself. This is true today and it will be true in two years when the tools have changed names.
53	
54	Two corollaries the training hammered:
55	
56	- **Claude is not autocomplete.** It's a co-engineer with memory and constraints — but the memory and the constraints are *things you supply*. It has no standards of its own. You are the standard.
57	- **Claude makes your assumptions visible faster.** That's the actual value. Not that it writes code — that it exposes the gap in your thinking in ten minutes instead of on Thursday night. Treat every gap it surfaces as a gift, not an insult.
58	
59	Everything else is mechanics in service of this.
60	
61	---
62	
63	## 2. The dual mandate
64	
65	You wear two hats *at the same time*, not in alternation. The failure mode is collapsing into one:
66	
67	- **Collapse into IC** → you ship your own components beautifully and the squad drifts, the rules layer rots, and nobody but you knows what "done" means.
68	- **Collapse into Lead** → you run great regroups and review everyone's work but haven't touched the codebase in three weeks, so your technical judgment goes stale and your reviews become vibes.
69	
70	Hold both. Here is the shift in each hat — same activity, two altitudes:
71	
72	| Dimension | As Individual Contributor | As Senior / Lead |
73	|---|---|---|
74	| **Think** | Get *this* component right — states, edges, what Claude will get wrong before it does. | Get the *system* right — will this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, go-live? |
75	| **Ask** | "What does this story not tell Claude Code?" | "What does our *rules layer* not tell any developer or any Claude instance on this project?" |
76	| **Communicate** | Precise AC, precise commit, precise "here's what Claude got wrong and why." | Frame reviews as work-not-person, translate across dev/BA/tester/SA, make commitments checkable. |
77	| **Decide** | Monolith or split *your* file, hook or component for *this* value — and defend it. | Set the *convention* the squad decides by, so nobody re-litigates it per component. |
78	| **Review** | Read your own output against the story before you commit. | Run the loop that makes *everyone's* output legible, and catch drift across the codebase. |
79	| **Think beyond** | The next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. | What happens when you're *not in the room*. The team you're growing. Maintainability in 2027. |
80	| **Protect** | Your commit doesn't introduce a hardcoded hex or an `any`. | The *whole codebase's* quality bar holds under deadline pressure — including when it's inconvenient. |
81	| **Multiply** | You get faster and cleaner. | The room gets faster and cleaner *because of how you work*. You are the capability anchor. |
82	
83	The training's own closing line for the cohort — *"This group is the capability anchor; the expectation is that what you learned reaches the people who weren't in this room"* — is a job description for the Lead hat. Internalize it.
84	
85	---
86	
87	## 3. Tooling model: two tools, two mindsets, one handoff
88	
89	The single most consequential distinction in the whole week:
90	
91	- **Claude.ai = the planning partner.** It explores, suggests, asks questions, thinks out loud with you. Use it to *decide*.
92	- **Claude Code = the engineering colleague in your terminal.** It reads files, writes code, runs commands. Critically: **it does not ask what you meant — it infers and proceeds.** Use it to *build*.
93	
94	**The handoff rule:** move from Claude.ai to Claude Code only *when you trust your plan enough to stop editing it and start building from it.* Not before.
95	
96	**The most common mistake — and it will tempt your whole squad:** moving to Claude Code too early because you're excited to build. Then Claude Code starts inventing things to fill the gaps you left, and by mid-sprint you're fighting the tool instead of directing it.
97	
98	- *IC discipline:* Don't open Claude Code on a story you haven't hardened. If you're still discovering questions, you're still in Claude.ai.
99	- *Lead discipline:* Watch for the squad jumping to build early. "Is your plan ready for that?" is the question you ask before anyone scaffolds. The moment Claude Code reads a plan and finds the gaps is the most important moment — make the squad *curious* about it, not defensive.
100	
101	---
102	
103	## 4. Defeating agreeableness — the skill the whole week is built on
104	
105	**Claude is optimised to be helpful, which means optimised to agree.** Left to its defaults it will praise a plan that produces unusable output. Agreeable defaults produce unchallenged assumptions, and unchallenged assumptions cost hours of rework on a real, fixed-price engagement.
106	
107	You break the default deliberately. Four techniques, each producing meaningfully different output. These are your reusable prompts — adapt the wording, keep the intent:
108	
109	1. **Role framing** — *"Act as a senior engineer whose job is to find flaws in plans before they reach production. Be direct. Don't soften criticism."*
110	2. **Steelman** — *"What is the strongest argument against this approach? What would go wrong if we built this exactly as described?"*
111	3. **Critique-first** — *"Before telling me what's good about this, list every weakness, gap, or assumption you're making. Weaknesses first, always."*
112	4. **Constraint injection** — *"Assume this goes to production at scale. Assume a QA engineer rejects it if there are no tests. Assume a designer rejects it if there are hardcoded values. Now review it."*
113	
114	**Set a persistent baseline at the account level.** Account instructions change Claude's default behaviour across *every* conversation. The working style this session describes — "lead with the point, flag the trade-off mid-response, challenge like a senior reviewing a PR" — is the target. What you actually have today is a *tool-configuration* baseline, not a committed instructions file: a global effort dial and a curated plugin list that already push back on rubber-stamping (see §16.2). That's a real approximation, but don't assume the gap is already closed — closing it deliberately means writing the actual instructions, not just configuring the tool around the edges.
115	
116	- *IC discipline:* Never accept the first response on anything that matters. If Claude found nothing wrong with your plan, that's a signal to apply technique 1 or 2, not a signal you're done.
117	- *Lead discipline:* Make anti-agreeableness a *team norm*, not your private trick. A squad that accepts Claude's first answer wholesale will produce a codebase full of unexamined assumptions. Teach the four techniques. Put them in the shared rules. Ask in regroup: *"What did Claude agree with that it shouldn't have?"*
118	
119	---
120	
121	## 5. Context and thread hygiene
122	
123	Long conversations degrade output. Every message carries the full history; on a long thread the relevant signal gets buried in noise and quality quietly drops.
124	
125	The rules:
126	
127	- **New conversation when the topic shifts.** Topics bleed across context and pollute each other.
128	- **Name conversations like files, not chat logs.** `checkout-fetch-pattern`, not "SFCC stuff." Treat them as a structured archive you can navigate.
129	- **Aim for 8–10 named, focused threads**, not one 80-message thread called "Zimmermann."
130	- **Claude.ai Projects share context across conversations** — use a Project for planning. **Claude Code uses the repo's rules/context files instead** (`CLAUDE.md` + the `.claude/` layer).
131	
132	- *IC discipline:* One topic per thread. The moment you notice yourself pasting unrelated context to "remind" Claude, you needed a new thread three messages ago.
133	- *Lead discipline:* At team scale, thread hygiene stops being about *your* signal and becomes about *shared* context. What lives in a personal thread is invisible to the squad; what needs to be shared belongs in the Project or the rules layer, not buried in someone's chat history. Decide, as lead, what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact — and make that call explicit so the team isn't guessing.
134	
135	---
136	
137	## 6. The planning layer — your codebase's constitution
138	
139	This is where the quality ceiling is actually set. In the training it was a `.claude/` structure; on your project it's the equivalent rules-and-context layer (section 16 maps the names).
140	
141	### `CLAUDE.md` is a contract, not a readme
142	
143	It tells Claude exactly **what to build**, **how to build it**, and **what NOT to do**. Claude Code reads it at the start of *every* session. It is the entry point every prompt begins from.
144	
145	- **Use Claude to *critique* the contract, not rewrite it.** Ask what's wrong; fix one problem at a time. If you let Claude rewrite it wholesale you get a file that reflects Claude's assumptions, not your decisions.
146	- **Each fix should change *structure or specificity*, not wording.** Polishing sentences is procrastination. If your edit didn't change what Claude can or can't do, it wasn't a real edit.
147	
148	### One topic per file — a hard rule
149	
150	If a file covers two things, Claude gets confused about which one applies. So: `build-spec.md`, `solution-architecture.md`, `auth-spec.md`, `design-system.md`, `api-patterns.md`, `component-registry.md` — one concern each. The training's own structure split a `brief/` folder (the *what* and *how*) from a `rules/` layer (the enforceable constraints Claude checks against).
151	
152	**Monolith vs split is a real decision.** Both are defensible *if you can defend it* — but the split is where a serious project lands. A monolithic file and a split set of files produce genuinely *different* Claude Code output. Know why you chose yours.
153	
154	### `build-log.md` is memory, not documentation
155	
156	Claude reads it at the start of every session to know what state the project is in and what's already been done. It is how a fresh Claude Code session — with no memory of yesterday — picks up where you left off.
157	
158	### Define "done" — or Claude Code never stops
159	
160	Claude Code with no stopping condition keeps building components forever. If your file doesn't say what "done" looks like, Claude will invent more work. **Where does your file say what done is?** If it doesn't, that's a bug in the plan, not the tool.
161	
162	- *IC discipline:* Before you build, three questions must be *yes*: does Claude know exactly what to build, exactly how, and exactly what not to do? If any is no, fix it before you open Claude Code.
163	- *Lead discipline:* The planning layer is the highest-leverage thing you own. **This is a system, not a personal note.** A rule that isn't checkable is an aspiration Claude will ignore — police the difference across the whole `rules/` layer. And because two squads read the same files, ambiguity here isn't one dev's rework, it's a fork in the codebase. Owning this well is worth more than any component you'll personally write.
164	
165	---
166	
167	## 7. Gap-hunting before the build
168	
169	**Find every gap before Claude Code does. Every gap in your planning files costs time in the build** — and on a fixed-price job, that time comes out of margin.
170	
171	**Use two reviewers with different mindsets, in order:**
172	
173	1. **Claude.ai first** — the conversational reviewer. Prompt it as a senior engineer handing the project to a junior who'll build it with Claude Code: *"Find every place Claude Code would have to make an assumption because I haven't told it what to do. Be specific. Don't be kind."*
174	2. **Claude Code second** — the builder's reviewer. *"Read all files. Do not write code yet. Tell me: every assumption you'd have to make; every instruction that conflicts with another; every topic the files don't cover; check framework versions are current LTS; check the sample code is correct and uses our methodology; any flaws with downstream impact. Reference the file and line for each."*
175	
176	**The contrast between what Claude.ai flags and what Claude Code flags is the lesson.** Claude.ai catches conceptual holes; Claude Code catches build-breaking ones. Whatever gaps remain after both — they're *knowable*, and knowable gaps are the ones you can close.
177	
178	**The distinction that separates real work from theatre:** *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* Acknowledging a gap in conversation and moving on is the seductive failure. Fixing means the file changed.
179	
180	- *IC discipline:* Run both reviewers on your own stories before you build. "What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?" is the most useful question you'll ask all day.
181	- *Lead discipline:* Institutionalize the two-reviewer pass as a squad ritual before any sprint. And guard against acknowledge-don't-fix at the team level — in review, don't ask "did Claude flag anything?", ask "show me the file line you changed."
182	
183	---
184	
185	## 8. Scaffolding discipline
186	
187	**Do not scaffold by hand.** Running the framework's project generator manually (`create-next-app` in training; the PWA Kit generator on your project) *skips the brief entirely* — Claude Code won't wire up your design tokens, routes, env vars, or folder structure, and you'll spend Wednesday paying for it.
188	
189	Instead: let Claude Code **read the brief and execute every setup step**, as an explicit numbered sequence — configure design tokens, set up fonts, create the folder structure from the architecture file, wire env placeholders, create the build-log with a setup checklist as its first entry. **Confirm each step; list every file created at the end.**
190	
191	- *IC discipline:* After generation, don't trust — verify. Open the token config; missing tokens cause compile errors downstream. A green scaffold checklist exists precisely so this moment is fast and unambiguous.
192	- *Lead discipline:* The scaffold sets conventions the whole squad inherits. Get the folder structure, token config, and env contract right *once*, centrally — every shortcut here is multiplied across every developer who builds on top of it.
193	
194	---
195	
196	## 9. The build loop — the core craft
197	
198	This is the part that "makes the methodology different from just prompting." Everything above exists to make this loop clean.
199	
200	### 9.1 Atomic design, bottom-up
201	
202	Build in layers: **layout primitives → atoms → molecules → components.** The lower layers are the foundation; you generate them from the design-system spec *first*, review them carefully, and everything above imports them.
203	
204	### 9.2 The story skill — consistency at scale
205	
206	A **skill is a reusable Claude prompt** that produces consistent, buildable output given a component name. You build one `story-skill` conversation and drive it with a command: `/create-story [ComponentName]`.
207	
208	A good story is **thin — intent and constraints, not implementation detail.** The non-negotiable format:
209	
210	- Follows the story template exactly.
211	- References the *correct* design file and the *correct* data stub (or none, for static components).
212	- **AC describes behaviour, not implementation** — something a tester can verify without asking a developer what it means.
213	- **Always includes happy path + loading-state AC + error-state AC.** Three states, every time.
214	- **Flags anything uncertain rather than inventing it.**
215	
216	**The skill is only as good as its prompt — and the prompt gets better every time you find a gap in its output.** Run it, find what it invented or left vague, refine one thing, run again. The second output is tighter. *That iteration is the lesson* — it's the same feedback loop as section 9.6, applied to your tooling.
217	
218	### 9.3 Generate is 10%. Review is 90%.
219	
220	Generating a component or a story takes a minute. **The work is the review.** A bad story generates a bad component; five minutes reviewing a story now saves an hour tonight.
221	
222	**Hard rule: no one builds from a story they haven't personally read and checked.** Not you, not anyone on the squad.
223	
224	### 9.4 The registry — import, don't reinvent
225	
226	`component-registry.md` lists what exists, where it lives, and its data source. Before building anything: **check the registry and import what's there — do not rebuild atoms inline.** After building: **update the registry.**
227	
228	The test: *"If Claude Code opens this repo tomorrow with no memory of today, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?"* On a solo project that's a convenience. **On two squads it's the difference between reuse and three developers building three different `StatusBadge`s.**
229	
230	### 9.5 The loop itself
231	
232	> **story → build → review → correct → commit.** One story, one prompt, one review, one commit.
233	
234	The build prompt pattern, every component: *read the registry, read the design-system rules, read this component's story, read the design file — confirm what you read before writing a single line of code — build exactly as specified, import from the registry, don't reinvent.*
235	
236	- *IC discipline:* Run the loop honestly on your own components. When Claude Code does something the story didn't specify, that's a defect in the story — go fix the story (9.6), don't just patch the code.
237	- *Lead discipline:* The loop is what you're teaching and enforcing. In review, verify the loop *ran*: "Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did you just hand it the design file?" A squad that skips the story and prompts from the design file is doing exactly the thing the methodology exists to prevent.
238	
239	### 9.6 The feedback loop that hardens the rules layer
240	
241	The most important habit for long-term quality:
242	
243	> **"Find one place where Claude Code made a decision you didn't specify. What would you add to the AC or the rules to prevent that next time?"**
244	
245	Every correction is data. A correction you make once and forget is a correction you'll make fifty times across the codebase. A correction you *push back into the story template or the rules layer* is made once, forever, for the whole squad. This is how the rules layer becomes real instead of aspirational — and it's pure Lead leverage.
246	
247	---
248	
249	## 10. The quality bar and the anti-patterns
250	
251	### The hardening checklist — every component, non-negotiable
252	
253	Run this on every component before it's "done." (Stack names are translated to your project; the *intent* is verbatim from training.)
254

263	### Anti-patterns to catch on sight
264	
265	- **Over-engineering.** A static banner that should be ~25–35 lines of JSX comes back as 120 — that's Claude over-engineering; simplify it. If a trivial component takes too long to build, the problem is usually the atom layer underneath, not the component.
266	- **Logic in the wrong place.** Derive calculated values (a `percentUsed`, a `daysRemaining`) **in the component, not the hook** — or wherever your `api-patterns` rule specifies. 267	- **Fetch inside the component.** Data-fetching follows the shared pattern (a hook / service layer), *not* inline in the component.
268	- **UI state vs server state confusion.** A local toggle is local UI state — it does not round-trip to the API. Know which is which and don't let Claude blur them.
269	- **Invented data sources.** A *derived* component (one whose data comes from other components' data) does not get its own stub or its own API call. If Claude invents one, **fix the story, not the code.**
270	- **Rebuilt assets.** Complex SVGs / illustrations get copied from the design file verbatim — don't let Claude "recreate" them from scratch.
271	- **Hardcoded-per-item logic.** Icon or variant selection driven by a `type` enum, not a hardcoded branch per item.

273	- *IC discipline:* Harden your own work to this bar before you'd dream of asking anyone else to.
274	- *Lead discipline:* This checklist is your review rubric and your definition of team-done. The over-engineering and drift checks especially are things *only a senior eye catches* — juniors accept whatever compiles. That catch is a large part of what you're paid for.

278	## 11. Shipping discipline — pragmatism under a fixed-price clock
279	
280	The training's pragmatism is directly relevant to a fixed-price, deadline-bound delivery:
281	
282	- **Deploy first.** A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible — to the review, to the client, to everyone. *"A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible to the regroup."*
283	- **A partial-but-hardened deliverable beats a complete-but-broken one.** *"A deployed page with a loading state beats a perfect local component."* *"A partial portal with hardened components beats a complete portal with broken states."*
284	- **Descope — never cut.** When something runs over: reduce scope (the complex chart becomes a data table — same data, no charting library), commit a loading-skeleton placeholder, and move on. **Never delete the component entirely.** Something honest in place beats a hole.
285	- **The 20-minute rule.** If a fix will take more than ~20 minutes right before a deadline, it's not worth doing before the milestone. Ship what's done and done well; log the rest.
286	- **Compare against the design, side by side.** Design file on one half of the screen, live URL on the other. Divergence you can't see, you can't fix.
287	
288	- *IC discipline:* Make the descope call on your own work early and without ego. Running over at the 80% mark? Stop, commit a clean placeholder, move on.
289	- *Lead discipline:* You own the *triage* across the squad — what gets hardened, what gets descoped, what gets cut for the milestone. Protecting the quality bar under deadline pressure is the specific test of whether you're actually leading or just hoping. Hold the bar when it's inconvenient; that's when it counts.

385	## 14. Rituals to run — review culture as delivery practice
386	
387	The training's *regroup* is your review culture. On the project you're the facilitator, under real stakes. Run it deliberately:
388	
389	- **Every work block gets a regroup.** Build, then look at real work together. The regroup exists *to learn from the work, not to judge the person who wrote it* — say that out loud and mean it. This norm is the whole thing; without it people hide their work and you lose visibility.
390	- **Rotate who's on screen.** Don't only review the confident volunteers — deliberately surface work from people who haven't been seen. (The training literally cold-picks, and bribes volunteers with snacks. Do the humane version: make it safe, make it normal, make it everyone.)
391	- **Ask structural questions, not surface ones.** "Is this well-written?" is the wrong question. "What will Claude *do* with this?" is the right one. Push people from fixing words to fixing structure.
392	- **Rolling verbal reviews, not just projector sessions.** One person shares one surprising flag; the room reacts. Cheap, frequent, low-ceremony.
393	- **The showcase is honest, not polished.** When you demo up or across, show what was *built*, not what you were *trying* to build. The single most valuable thing to surface is *"one thing the AI got right that followed from our rules, and one thing we corrected and why"* — the correction is the more important half. Model this; it sets the honesty bar for the squad.
394	- **Commitments are specific enough to check.** "Use Claude more" is not a commitment. *"Write the AC before I open Claude Code, not after"* is. Hold yourself and the squad to actionable specificity — the kind someone could verify in three months.

Your job takes that methodology into **shared-codebase, two-squad, fixed-price delivery on a stack you don't yet have deep muscle memory in.** The discipline carries over completely. The framework fluency and the leadership craft are the two things you have to build deliberately on top of it.
493	
494	What's different now versus when this section was first written: you're no longer bridging from a solution deck. The repo is real, most of what it needed has already been read once, end to end, and the gaps that remain (§16.2's corrections, §16.4's contradictions) are *knowable* — which, per §7, means they're closeable. This document is only useful if you actually close them, not just read that they exist.
495	
496	The quality ceiling is set by you. So set it high, and hold it when it's inconvenient.
