> # ⚠️ ARCHIVED — 25 August 2026
>
> **This document is retired and no longer maintained.** It was written 9 July 2026 from the
> Manila AI-engineering training week, whose vehicle was a Next.js / Tailwind / Contentful
> stack — not this project's Salesforce PWA Kit.
>
> **Its durable operating principles moved to `fedLead-playbook.md` §3 (Principles) and §4
> (Working with AI tooling).** The training-vehicle material was dropped rather than migrated:
> its artifacts (`build-log.md`, `component-registry.md`, the story skill) were training
> fixtures, and §16.1 of this document already conceded three of them were imagined.
>
> Kept on disk for provenance. Several claims below are contradicted by the current codebase —
> most notably that the generated registry "can't go stale" (its tier column is unreliable),
> that hardcoded hex values are mechanically checkable (they weren't until 23 Aug, and the
> script still isn't in CI), and that deployment parity is manual discipline (every branch now
> auto-deploys to its own MRT environment).
>
> **Do not cite this file.** Use `fedLead-playbook.md`, `fedBuild-manual.md`, or
> `uiBuild-knowledge.md`.

---

# The Frontend Development Lead Playbook
### Zimmermann Commerce Migration · How to be the FE Lead as both IC and Senior/Lead

*Distilled from the Manila AI Engineering Training Week (June 2026, facilitated by Tim Lavelle). This is your operating manual, not a summary of the week.*

---

## 0. How to use this document

This is the standard you hold yourself and your squad to. Read it once end-to-end, then treat it as a lookup — every section is written so you can jump to it mid-delivery.

**Source and provenance — read this once so you never confuse the two layers:**

- Everything in sections 1–9 is grounded in the **Manila training**. The training vehicle was a *TelcoNow B2C portal* on **Next.js 14 · TypeScript · Tailwind · Contentful**. That is what was actually taught.
- The training's *methodology* is deliberately stack-agnostic. Its closing thesis: **"The discipline transfers. The specific tools won't."** That is why it maps onto Zimmermann at all.
- Anything about **SFCC / PWA Kit / MRT / the two squads / RACI / CI-CD gates / integrations** is **me bridging to your project** from separate context (the solution deck and project setup). It is labeled as a bridge in **section 16**, which has since been verified against the real repo (2026-07-09) — corrections and open items are called out there, not silently folded in here. Don't cite section 16 as training content; it still isn't.

**The three gaps you carry into this role — stated plainly, because pretending they aren't there is how leads fail:**

1. **Framework gap.** You're Angular-primary. The training and the project are React (Next in training, PWA Kit in project). The *habits* below transfer cleanly. The *code idioms* do not. Build PWA Kit / React fluency as a separate, explicit track — don't let the transferable methodology fool you into thinking the framework transfers with it.
2. **Scale gap.** The training taught *solo* builds. You lead *shared-codebase, two-squad* delivery. Every "memory for future-you" artifact below has to be re-read as "contract for the whole team." Section 16 makes that jump concrete.
3. **Leadership gap.** You are stepping up into the lead seat. The IC craft you already have. The lead craft — running review culture, protecting quality under pressure, multiplying yourself — is the part this document is really for.

---

## 1. The one principle everything hangs on

> **The quality ceiling is set by the human, not the AI.**

Claude will match the quality of what you give it. Give it a vague plan, you get plausible garbage that costs hours to unwind. Give it a tight contract, sharp stories, and enforced rules, and you get output you'd have been proud to write yourself. This is true today and it will be true in two years when the tools have changed names.

Two corollaries the training hammered:

- **Claude is not autocomplete.** It's a co-engineer with memory and constraints — but the memory and the constraints are *things you supply*. It has no standards of its own. You are the standard.
- **Claude makes your assumptions visible faster.** That's the actual value. Not that it writes code — that it exposes the gap in your thinking in ten minutes instead of on Thursday night. Treat every gap it surfaces as a gift, not an insult.

Everything else is mechanics in service of this.

---

## 2. The dual mandate

You wear two hats *at the same time*, not in alternation. The failure mode is collapsing into one:

- **Collapse into IC** → you ship your own components beautifully and the squad drifts, the rules layer rots, and nobody but you knows what "done" means.
- **Collapse into Lead** → you run great regroups and review everyone's work but haven't touched the codebase in three weeks, so your technical judgment goes stale and your reviews become vibes.

Hold both. Here is the shift in each hat — same activity, two altitudes:

| Dimension | As Individual Contributor | As Senior / Lead |
|---|---|---|
| **Think** | Get *this* component right — states, edges, what Claude will get wrong before it does. | Get the *system* right — will this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, go-live? |
| **Ask** | "What does this story not tell Claude Code?" | "What does our *rules layer* not tell any developer or any Claude instance on this project?" |
| **Communicate** | Precise AC, precise commit, precise "here's what Claude got wrong and why." | Frame reviews as work-not-person, translate across dev/BA/tester/SA, make commitments checkable. |
| **Decide** | Monolith or split *your* file, hook or component for *this* value — and defend it. | Set the *convention* the squad decides by, so nobody re-litigates it per component. |
| **Review** | Read your own output against the story before you commit. | Run the loop that makes *everyone's* output legible, and catch drift across the codebase. |
| **Think beyond** | The next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. | What happens when you're *not in the room*. The team you're growing. Maintainability in 2027. |
| **Protect** | Your commit doesn't introduce a hardcoded hex or an `any`. | The *whole codebase's* quality bar holds under deadline pressure — including when it's inconvenient. |
| **Multiply** | You get faster and cleaner. | The room gets faster and cleaner *because of how you work*. You are the capability anchor. |

The training's own closing line for the cohort — *"This group is the capability anchor; the expectation is that what you learned reaches the people who weren't in this room"* — is a job description for the Lead hat. Internalize it.

---

## 3. Tooling model: two tools, two mindsets, one handoff

The single most consequential distinction in the whole week:

- **Claude.ai = the planning partner.** It explores, suggests, asks questions, thinks out loud with you. Use it to *decide*.
- **Claude Code = the engineering colleague in your terminal.** It reads files, writes code, runs commands. Critically: **it does not ask what you meant — it infers and proceeds.** Use it to *build*.

**The handoff rule:** move from Claude.ai to Claude Code only *when you trust your plan enough to stop editing it and start building from it.* Not before.

**The most common mistake — and it will tempt your whole squad:** moving to Claude Code too early because you're excited to build. Then Claude Code starts inventing things to fill the gaps you left, and by mid-sprint you're fighting the tool instead of directing it.

- *IC discipline:* Don't open Claude Code on a story you haven't hardened. If you're still discovering questions, you're still in Claude.ai.
- *Lead discipline:* Watch for the squad jumping to build early. "Is your plan ready for that?" is the question you ask before anyone scaffolds. The moment Claude Code reads a plan and finds the gaps is the most important moment — make the squad *curious* about it, not defensive.

---

## 4. Defeating agreeableness — the skill the whole week is built on

**Claude is optimised to be helpful, which means optimised to agree.** Left to its defaults it will praise a plan that produces unusable output. Agreeable defaults produce unchallenged assumptions, and unchallenged assumptions cost hours of rework on a real, fixed-price engagement.

You break the default deliberately. Four techniques, each producing meaningfully different output. These are your reusable prompts — adapt the wording, keep the intent:

1. **Role framing** — *"Act as a senior engineer whose job is to find flaws in plans before they reach production. Be direct. Don't soften criticism."*
2. **Steelman** — *"What is the strongest argument against this approach? What would go wrong if we built this exactly as described?"*
3. **Critique-first** — *"Before telling me what's good about this, list every weakness, gap, or assumption you're making. Weaknesses first, always."*
4. **Constraint injection** — *"Assume this goes to production at scale. Assume a QA engineer rejects it if there are no tests. Assume a designer rejects it if there are hardcoded values. Now review it."*

**Set a persistent baseline at the account level.** Account instructions change Claude's default behaviour across *every* conversation. The working style this session describes — "lead with the point, flag the trade-off mid-response, challenge like a senior reviewing a PR" — is the target. What you actually have today is a *tool-configuration* baseline, not a committed instructions file: a global effort dial and a curated plugin list that already push back on rubber-stamping (see §16.2). That's a real approximation, but don't assume the gap is already closed — closing it deliberately means writing the actual instructions, not just configuring the tool around the edges.

- *IC discipline:* Never accept the first response on anything that matters. If Claude found nothing wrong with your plan, that's a signal to apply technique 1 or 2, not a signal you're done.
- *Lead discipline:* Make anti-agreeableness a *team norm*, not your private trick. A squad that accepts Claude's first answer wholesale will produce a codebase full of unexamined assumptions. Teach the four techniques. Put them in the shared rules. Ask in regroup: *"What did Claude agree with that it shouldn't have?"*

---

## 5. Context and thread hygiene

Long conversations degrade output. Every message carries the full history; on a long thread the relevant signal gets buried in noise and quality quietly drops.

The rules:

- **New conversation when the topic shifts.** Topics bleed across context and pollute each other.
- **Name conversations like files, not chat logs.** `checkout-fetch-pattern`, not "SFCC stuff." Treat them as a structured archive you can navigate.
- **Aim for 8–10 named, focused threads**, not one 80-message thread called "Zimmermann."
- **Claude.ai Projects share context across conversations** — use a Project for planning. **Claude Code uses the repo's rules/context files instead** (`CLAUDE.md` + the `.claude/` layer).

- *IC discipline:* One topic per thread. The moment you notice yourself pasting unrelated context to "remind" Claude, you needed a new thread three messages ago.
- *Lead discipline:* At team scale, thread hygiene stops being about *your* signal and becomes about *shared* context. What lives in a personal thread is invisible to the squad; what needs to be shared belongs in the Project or the rules layer, not buried in someone's chat history. Decide, as lead, what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact — and make that call explicit so the team isn't guessing.

---

## 6. The planning layer — your codebase's constitution

This is where the quality ceiling is actually set. In the training it was a `.claude/` structure; on your project it's the equivalent rules-and-context layer (section 16 maps the names).

### `CLAUDE.md` is a contract, not a readme

It tells Claude exactly **what to build**, **how to build it**, and **what NOT to do**. Claude Code reads it at the start of *every* session. It is the entry point every prompt begins from.

- **Use Claude to *critique* the contract, not rewrite it.** Ask what's wrong; fix one problem at a time. If you let Claude rewrite it wholesale you get a file that reflects Claude's assumptions, not your decisions.
- **Each fix should change *structure or specificity*, not wording.** Polishing sentences is procrastination. If your edit didn't change what Claude can or can't do, it wasn't a real edit.

### One topic per file — a hard rule

If a file covers two things, Claude gets confused about which one applies. So: `build-spec.md`, `solution-architecture.md`, `auth-spec.md`, `design-system.md`, `api-patterns.md`, `component-registry.md` — one concern each. The training's own structure split a `brief/` folder (the *what* and *how*) from a `rules/` layer (the enforceable constraints Claude checks against).

**Monolith vs split is a real decision.** Both are defensible *if you can defend it* — but the split is where a serious project lands. A monolithic file and a split set of files produce genuinely *different* Claude Code output. Know why you chose yours.

### `build-log.md` is memory, not documentation

Claude reads it at the start of every session to know what state the project is in and what's already been done. It is how a fresh Claude Code session — with no memory of yesterday — picks up where you left off.

### Define "done" — or Claude Code never stops

Claude Code with no stopping condition keeps building components forever. If your file doesn't say what "done" looks like, Claude will invent more work. **Where does your file say what done is?** If it doesn't, that's a bug in the plan, not the tool.

- *IC discipline:* Before you build, three questions must be *yes*: does Claude know exactly what to build, exactly how, and exactly what not to do? If any is no, fix it before you open Claude Code.
- *Lead discipline:* The planning layer is the highest-leverage thing you own. **This is a system, not a personal note.** A rule that isn't checkable is an aspiration Claude will ignore — police the difference across the whole `rules/` layer. And because two squads read the same files, ambiguity here isn't one dev's rework, it's a fork in the codebase. Owning this well is worth more than any component you'll personally write.

---

## 7. Gap-hunting before the build

**Find every gap before Claude Code does. Every gap in your planning files costs time in the build** — and on a fixed-price job, that time comes out of margin.

**Use two reviewers with different mindsets, in order:**

1. **Claude.ai first** — the conversational reviewer. Prompt it as a senior engineer handing the project to a junior who'll build it with Claude Code: *"Find every place Claude Code would have to make an assumption because I haven't told it what to do. Be specific. Don't be kind."*
2. **Claude Code second** — the builder's reviewer. *"Read all files. Do not write code yet. Tell me: every assumption you'd have to make; every instruction that conflicts with another; every topic the files don't cover; check framework versions are current LTS; check the sample code is correct and uses our methodology; any flaws with downstream impact. Reference the file and line for each."*

**The contrast between what Claude.ai flags and what Claude Code flags is the lesson.** Claude.ai catches conceptual holes; Claude Code catches build-breaking ones. Whatever gaps remain after both — they're *knowable*, and knowable gaps are the ones you can close.

**The distinction that separates real work from theatre:** *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* Acknowledging a gap in conversation and moving on is the seductive failure. Fixing means the file changed.

- *IC discipline:* Run both reviewers on your own stories before you build. "What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?" is the most useful question you'll ask all day.
- *Lead discipline:* Institutionalize the two-reviewer pass as a squad ritual before any sprint. And guard against acknowledge-don't-fix at the team level — in review, don't ask "did Claude flag anything?", ask "show me the file line you changed."

---

## 8. Scaffolding discipline

**Do not scaffold by hand.** Running the framework's project generator manually (`create-next-app` in training; the PWA Kit generator on your project) *skips the brief entirely* — Claude Code won't wire up your design tokens, routes, env vars, or folder structure, and you'll spend Wednesday paying for it.

Instead: let Claude Code **read the brief and execute every setup step**, as an explicit numbered sequence — configure design tokens, set up fonts, create the folder structure from the architecture file, wire env placeholders, create the build-log with a setup checklist as its first entry. **Confirm each step; list every file created at the end.**

- *IC discipline:* After generation, don't trust — verify. Open the token config; missing tokens cause compile errors downstream. A green scaffold checklist exists precisely so this moment is fast and unambiguous.
- *Lead discipline:* The scaffold sets conventions the whole squad inherits. Get the folder structure, token config, and env contract right *once*, centrally — every shortcut here is multiplied across every developer who builds on top of it.

---

## 9. The build loop — the core craft

This is the part that "makes the methodology different from just prompting." Everything above exists to make this loop clean.

### 9.1 Atomic design, bottom-up

Build in layers: **layout primitives → atoms → molecules → components.** The lower layers are the foundation; you generate them from the design-system spec *first*, review them carefully, and everything above imports them.

### 9.2 The story skill — consistency at scale

A **skill is a reusable Claude prompt** that produces consistent, buildable output given a component name. You build one `story-skill` conversation and drive it with a command: `/create-story [ComponentName]`.

A good story is **thin — intent and constraints, not implementation detail.** The non-negotiable format:

- Follows the story template exactly.
- References the *correct* design file and the *correct* data stub (or none, for static components).
- **AC describes behaviour, not implementation** — something a tester can verify without asking a developer what it means.
- **Always includes happy path + loading-state AC + error-state AC.** Three states, every time.
- **Flags anything uncertain rather than inventing it.**

**The skill is only as good as its prompt — and the prompt gets better every time you find a gap in its output.** Run it, find what it invented or left vague, refine one thing, run again. The second output is tighter. *That iteration is the lesson* — it's the same feedback loop as section 9.6, applied to your tooling.

### 9.3 Generate is 10%. Review is 90%.

Generating a component or a story takes a minute. **The work is the review.** A bad story generates a bad component; five minutes reviewing a story now saves an hour tonight.

**Hard rule: no one builds from a story they haven't personally read and checked.** Not you, not anyone on the squad.

### 9.4 The registry — import, don't reinvent

`component-registry.md` lists what exists, where it lives, and its data source. Before building anything: **check the registry and import what's there — do not rebuild atoms inline.** After building: **update the registry.**

The test: *"If Claude Code opens this repo tomorrow with no memory of today, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?"* On a solo project that's a convenience. **On two squads it's the difference between reuse and three developers building three different `StatusBadge`s.**

### 9.5 The loop itself

> **story → build → review → correct → commit.** One story, one prompt, one review, one commit.

The build prompt pattern, every component: *read the registry, read the design-system rules, read this component's story, read the design file — confirm what you read before writing a single line of code — build exactly as specified, import from the registry, don't reinvent.*

- *IC discipline:* Run the loop honestly on your own components. When Claude Code does something the story didn't specify, that's a defect in the story — go fix the story (9.6), don't just patch the code.
- *Lead discipline:* The loop is what you're teaching and enforcing. In review, verify the loop *ran*: "Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did you just hand it the design file?" A squad that skips the story and prompts from the design file is doing exactly the thing the methodology exists to prevent.

### 9.6 The feedback loop that hardens the rules layer

The most important habit for long-term quality:

> **"Find one place where Claude Code made a decision you didn't specify. What would you add to the AC or the rules to prevent that next time?"**

Every correction is data. A correction you make once and forget is a correction you'll make fifty times across the codebase. A correction you *push back into the story template or the rules layer* is made once, forever, for the whole squad. This is how the rules layer becomes real instead of aspirational — and it's pure Lead leverage.

---

## 10. The quality bar and the anti-patterns

### The hardening checklist — every component, non-negotiable

Run this on every component before it's "done." (Stack names are translated to your project; the *intent* is verbatim from training.)

- **Mobile layout at 375px** — actually open dev tools and check.
- **Loading state present — a skeleton, not a spinner.**
- **Error state present — a proper error component *with retry*.**
- **No hardcoded hex values — design tokens only.**
- **No TypeScript `any`** — strict mode on. *(This is already your default per your working style — hold the squad to it.)*
- **Deployed and resolving — matches local, not just running locally.**
- **Registry updated with everything built.**

### Anti-patterns to catch on sight

- **Over-engineering.** A static banner that should be ~25–35 lines of JSX comes back as 120 — that's Claude over-engineering; simplify it. If a trivial component takes too long to build, the problem is usually the atom layer underneath, not the component.
- **Logic in the wrong place.** Derive calculated values (a `percentUsed`, a `daysRemaining`) **in the component, not the hook** — or wherever your `api-patterns` rule specifies. The point isn't the specific rule; it's *consistency* — watch for Claude Code *drifting* from the pattern across components.
- **Fetch inside the component.** Data-fetching follows the shared pattern (a hook / service layer), *not* inline in the component.
- **UI state vs server state confusion.** A local toggle is local UI state — it does not round-trip to the API. Know which is which and don't let Claude blur them.
- **Invented data sources.** A *derived* component (one whose data comes from other components' data) does not get its own stub or its own API call. If Claude invents one, **fix the story, not the code.**
- **Rebuilt assets.** Complex SVGs / illustrations get copied from the design file verbatim — don't let Claude "recreate" them from scratch.
- **Hardcoded-per-item logic.** Icon or variant selection driven by a `type` enum, not a hardcoded branch per item.

- *IC discipline:* Harden your own work to this bar before you'd dream of asking anyone else to.
- *Lead discipline:* This checklist is your review rubric and your definition of team-done. The over-engineering and drift checks especially are things *only a senior eye catches* — juniors accept whatever compiles. That catch is a large part of what you're paid for.

---

## 11. Shipping discipline — pragmatism under a fixed-price clock

The training's pragmatism is directly relevant to a fixed-price, deadline-bound delivery:

- **Deploy first.** A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible — to the review, to the client, to everyone. *"A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible to the regroup."*
- **A partial-but-hardened deliverable beats a complete-but-broken one.** *"A deployed page with a loading state beats a perfect local component."* *"A partial portal with hardened components beats a complete portal with broken states."*
- **Descope — never cut.** When something runs over: reduce scope (the complex chart becomes a data table — same data, no charting library), commit a loading-skeleton placeholder, and move on. **Never delete the component entirely.** Something honest in place beats a hole.
- **The 20-minute rule.** If a fix will take more than ~20 minutes right before a deadline, it's not worth doing before the milestone. Ship what's done and done well; log the rest.
- **Compare against the design, side by side.** Design file on one half of the screen, live URL on the other. Divergence you can't see, you can't fix.

- *IC discipline:* Make the descope call on your own work early and without ego. Running over at the 80% mark? Stop, commit a clean placeholder, move on.
- *Lead discipline:* You own the *triage* across the squad — what gets hardened, what gets descoped, what gets cut for the milestone. Protecting the quality bar under deadline pressure is the specific test of whether you're actually leading or just hoping. Hold the bar when it's inconvenient; that's when it counts.

---

## 12. Cross-cutting dimensions — the "etc."

The user asked for the *etc.* explicitly. Here is the full dual-lens reference — the same eleven capabilities, each in both hats. This is the section to reread before a hard week.

**Think.**
IC — one component deep: states, edges, and *what Claude will get wrong before it does.* Lead — one system wide: does this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, the go-live sequence, maintainability in 2027?

**Ask.** *(full question bank in section 13)*
IC — the questions that expose gaps in *a story*. Lead — the questions that expose gaps in *the rules layer, the conventions, and the team's understanding.*

**Communicate.**
IC — precise AC, precise commits, precise "here's what Claude got right and what I corrected and why" (specificity over politeness — the *correction* is the more valuable half). Flag uncertainty; never invent. Lead — frame reviews as *work-not-person*; translate across dev/BA/tester/SA; keep the showcase *honest, not polished*; make every commitment specific enough that someone could check it in three months.

**Decide.**
IC — monolith-or-split for *your* files, hook-or-component for *this* value — and be able to defend it. Lead — set the *convention* so the squad doesn't re-litigate the same decision every component; document it in the rules layer.

**Review.**
IC — your own output against the story, before commit, honestly. Lead — run the loop that makes *everyone's* work legible; catch pattern-drift across the codebase that no single-component view reveals.

**Ship.**
IC — deploy your own work, descope early, no ego. Lead — triage what hardens / descopes / cuts across the whole squad against the milestone.

**Improve.**
IC — every correction you make, push back into your story or prompt so you never make it twice. Lead — push corrections into the *shared* rules layer so the *squad* never makes them again. This is your highest-leverage move.

**Protect quality.**
IC — your commit is clean (no `any`, no hex, three states). Lead — the bar holds across the codebase *under deadline pressure*, including when holding it is inconvenient.

**Manage context.**
IC — one topic per thread; named threads; short threads. Lead — decide what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact and make it explicit, so team knowledge lives in the Project and rules layer, not in someone's chat history.

**Handle uncertainty.**
IC — flag what you (or Claude) are unsure of rather than inventing; distinguish "verified" from "assumed." *(This is already how you work — it's your verification mindset. Keep it.)* Lead — make "flag, don't invent" a team norm; keep an open-items list visible; never let an assumption harden into a fact silently.

**Multiply / mentor.**
IC — you get faster and cleaner. Lead — *the room* gets faster and cleaner because of how you work. You are the capability anchor; knowledge you don't transfer is a single point of failure wearing your name.

**Think beyond.**
IC — the next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. Lead — what happens when you're *not in the room*: the team you're growing, the second squad's dependencies, the integration seams, the go-live risk, the two-year maintainability of every convention you set.

---

## 13. The questions bank

Extracted straight from the training's regroup and review prompts, re-pointed for your project and split by hat. Keep these where you can grab them.

### Questions you ask yourself / Claude (IC hat)

**Planning a story or file:**
- What would a senior engineer need to know that this file doesn't tell them?
- What assumption would Claude Code make here that isn't written down?
- Is this a rule Claude can *check against*, or an aspiration it will ignore?
- What's missing that would cause the first build to go wrong?
- Where does this say what "done" looks like?

**After Claude reviews your plan:**
- What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?
- Is that *fixed* now, or did I just *acknowledge* it?
- If Claude Code reads this tonight and I'm not around — what goes wrong?

**Reviewing your own output:**
- Does this AC describe *behaviour a tester can verify*, or implementation?
- Is there a loading-state AC? An error-state AC?
- Did Claude Code follow the story, or invent something? What, exactly?
- Did I check the registry before building — what was already there that I reused?
- Where's this calculated — hook or component? Is that consistent with the pattern?
- Find one decision Claude made that the story didn't specify. What do I add to prevent it next time?

### Questions you ask the squad / the codebase (Lead hat)

**On the rules layer:**
- What would *any* developer assume here that isn't written down?
- Is this a checkable rule or an aspiration? *(ask it of the whole rules layer, not one story)*
- If a fresh Claude Code session opens this repo with no memory, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?
- What did Claude.ai miss that Claude Code found? What's the *pattern*?

**In regroup / review:**
- What's working here — specific enough for Claude to act on?
- What's still missing or too vague to be useful?
- Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did someone just hand it the design file?
- Show me one AC line and where it appears in the build.
- Did you have to correct Claude Code? Could the story have prevented it?
- Four components in — is Claude Code consistent with our patterns, or drifting?

**Cross-role and forward-looking:**
- (To BAs/testers) Was there a component where the AC wasn't testable? What would you write instead?
- What did Claude do *consistently* wrong across multiple components? *(that's a rules-layer fix, not fifty code fixes)*
- Did the rules layer actually change Claude Code's output, or are we correcting the same things anyway?
- What's the thing no one has said yet that everyone is thinking?

---

## 14. Rituals to run — review culture as delivery practice

The training's *regroup* is your review culture. On the project you're the facilitator, under real stakes. Run it deliberately:

- **Every work block gets a regroup.** Build, then look at real work together. The regroup exists *to learn from the work, not to judge the person who wrote it* — say that out loud and mean it. This norm is the whole thing; without it people hide their work and you lose visibility.
- **Rotate who's on screen.** Don't only review the confident volunteers — deliberately surface work from people who haven't been seen. (The training literally cold-picks, and bribes volunteers with snacks. Do the humane version: make it safe, make it normal, make it everyone.)
- **Ask structural questions, not surface ones.** "Is this well-written?" is the wrong question. "What will Claude *do* with this?" is the right one. Push people from fixing words to fixing structure.
- **Rolling verbal reviews, not just projector sessions.** One person shares one surprising flag; the room reacts. Cheap, frequent, low-ceremony.
- **The showcase is honest, not polished.** When you demo up or across, show what was *built*, not what you were *trying* to build. The single most valuable thing to surface is *"one thing the AI got right that followed from our rules, and one thing we corrected and why"* — the correction is the more important half. Model this; it sets the honesty bar for the squad.
- **Commitments are specific enough to check.** "Use Claude more" is not a commitment. *"Write the AC before I open Claude Code, not after"* is. Hold yourself and the squad to actionable specificity — the kind someone could verify in three months.

---

## 15. How you'll know you're slipping

Failure signals, by hat. If you catch these in yourself, correct before they compound.

**IC drift:**
- You accept Claude's first response on things that matter.
- You're editing wording in your planning files instead of structure.
- You built a component without reading its story, or without checking the registry.
- You corrected Claude and moved on without fixing the story.
- You have one 60-message thread called "Zimmermann."

**Lead drift:**
- You haven't touched the codebase in weeks — your reviews are becoming vibes.
- Your rules layer has aspirations in it that Claude Code demonstrably ignores.
- You're fixing the same Claude mistake in five components instead of fixing it once in the rules.
- Reviews feel like judging people, and people have started hiding their work.
- You're the only one who knows how a convention works — you haven't transferred it.
- Under deadline you quietly dropped the quality bar and didn't say so.

### 16.4 Your first gap-hunts — live, unresolved contradictions

Section 7 says to find every gap before Claude Code does. Here are four already sitting in the repo, found by cross-referencing real sources against each other. None are resolved below — that's deliberate, and it's a call for you and the leads, not something to silently pick a side on in a document.

**1. Who owns Home, PDP, and PLP?**
- `squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, and `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` all say **Squad A** — but `squadA.md` and `squadB.md` both self-label *"Draft squad split — scope can still change as sprints are confirmed,"* which is a real reason to weight them lower, not just a hedge.
- Root `CODEOWNERS` and the auto-generated `.claude/registry/pages.md` say **Squad B** — and unlike the draft rule files, these two are the mechanically current, enforced sources.
- Three skills (`onboarding`, `feature-spec`, `qa-generate`) also say Squad B, but don't count that as three independent checks — it's the same assumption hardcoded into all three prompts. It's not academic: `onboarding`'s actual interactive script tells a new Squad B developer, unconditionally, that they own `product-detail/` and `product-list/`. If Squad A turns out to be correct, this skill is actively misinforming every new hire today, not just disagreeing on paper.
- Everyone agrees cart/checkout is Squad A and search/account is Squad B — the fault line is specifically Home/PDP/PLP.

**2. May Claude write directly to memory and rules files, or must it always propose first?**
- `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`, a Stop hook, says Claude must *never* edit `.docs/memory/*`, `.claude/rules/*`, or PRDs directly — only draft a dated proposal into `.docs/agents-proposals/` for a human to review and apply by hand.
- `.claude/skills/session-start`'s own instructions describe writing to memory files directly, the moment something worth recording comes up.
- `frozenFiles.md`'s Tier-1 governance list doesn't include `.docs/memory/*` at all — the file-protection tier that would normally justify the hook's "never direct-edit" stance.
- This one is sharper than #1 — it's not just about who reviews a PR, it's about what Claude is actually allowed to do unprompted on this repo, and the answer currently depends on which doc a session happens to read first.

**3. Are the `.docs/prompts/` build-prompt templates actually "done"?**
- All three carry a `Status — done. Kept for traceability.` banner.
- Each one lists doc-artifact paths under a bare `docs/` directory as part of what it produced — and that directory doesn't exist anywhere in this repo. (The code/config artifacts they describe — `digital-sit.yml`, `playwright.config.js`, `.browserstack.yml`, and others — are all real and verified; only the documentation half of the "done" claim is stale, likely left behind by the project's later move to Confluence.)
- This is the literal version of §7's own question: *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* These files acknowledged a plan and marked themselves done. Nobody went back to check.

**4. Does `/code-quality`'s own default command even run?**
- Its `SKILL.md` says: if no argument is given, run `git diff --name-only main`.
- Run that in this repo today and git errors immediately — `fatal: ambiguous argument 'main': unknown revision or path not in the working tree` — there is no local `main` branch, only `develop`.
- Even where `main` resolves (say, after a fetch), it's the wrong base per `AGENTS.md`'s own Branch Rules table: `feature/*` and `fix/*` branch from `develop`, so diffing against `main` would pull in everything already merged to `develop` from unrelated, already-finished work.
- `/pr-checklist`, which calls `/code-quality` internally, gets this right — it diffs against `develop`. The two skills disagree with each other, and the one most people would reach for on its own is the one that's broken.

All four are the "is this a rule Claude can check against, or an aspiration it will ignore" failure mode from §6 — except worse, because each would pass a casual read. #1 would route a PR to the wrong reviewer, or actively misinform a new hire on day one. #2 means two Claude Code sessions on this same repo could legitimately behave differently depending on which rule they happened to read first. #3 means a document you'd otherwise trust as "done" is quietly missing half of what it claims. #4 means the tool you'd reach for to check your own work fails outright unless you already know to pass it an argument. Acknowledging all four in this paragraph isn't the fix, per §7's own distinction — the fix is whichever file actually changes.

### 16.5 The honest close

The training gave you a *transferable methodology* and proved it on a solo React build. Your job takes that methodology into **shared-codebase, two-squad, fixed-price delivery on a stack you don't yet have deep muscle memory in.** The discipline carries over completely. The framework fluency and the leadership craft are the two things you have to build deliberately on top of it.

What's different now versus when this section was first written: you're no longer bridging from a solution deck. The repo is real, most of what it needed has already been read once, end to end, and the gaps that remain (§16.2's corrections, §16.4's contradictions) are *knowable* — which, per §7, means they're closeable. This document is only useful if you actually close them, not just read that they exist.

The quality ceiling is set by you. So set it high, and hold it when it's inconvenient.

18	### The pipeline is one-way

22	        ↓

43	### The registration reality — this is the one that breaks layouts
44	
45	`theme/index.ts` registers the Zimmermann scale as **`space` only** (line 56). `sizes`,
46	`fontSizes`, `lineHeights` and `letterSpacings` are deliberately **not** registered, because
47	registering them would restyle the base retail-react-app at ~199 call sites.
48	
49	| Prop family | Reads | Bare key like `'xl'` |
50	|---|---|---|
51	| `margin` `padding` `gap` | `theme.space` ✅ registered | correct |
52	| `width` `height` `boxSize` `min/maxWidth/Height` | `theme.sizes` ❌ not registered | **falls through to Chakra's defaults** |
53	| `fontSize` `lineHeight` `letterSpacing` | ❌ not registered | wrong value, or nothing |
54	
55	Measured blow-up range: **8×–112×**. `width: 'xl'` resolves through `theme.sizes.xl` = 36rem
56	= **576px** — that shipped, blew the footer contact icons to 576px, and destroyed the layout

83	<Box color="text.default" padding="m" />

116	Before replacing a literal with a token, three checks — all three must pass:
117

123	   never in JSX or a recipe.

162	**1. `extendTheme` deep-merges — it does not replace.** A recipe named `Footer` merges into
163	base SFCC's `Footer` rather than replacing it, inheriting parts you never wrote. Namespace
164	everything: `ZimmFooter`, not `Footer`. `recipeGuards.test.ts` enforces this with
165	`INTENTIONAL_MERGES = ['Button', 'Header', 'ListMenu']` — those three are deliberate; anything
166	else must be namespaced.
167	
168	**1b. The merge reorders keys.** A key that already exists in the base keeps the **base's**
169	position in the merged object; a key you add that the base lacks is appended **last**. That is
170	the mechanism behind a shorthand resetting a longhand you wrote first — the order in your file
171	is not the order that ships. Inspect what actually applies:
172	
173	```js
174	theme.components.Header.baseStyle   // merged — what actually applies
175	```
176	
177	**2. A recipe unit test cannot catch the merge.** `extendTheme` does **not** populate
178	`theme.__cssMap` — only `ChakraProvider` does, via `toCSSVar`. So a direct `css()(theme)`
179	assertion in Vitest passes vacuously against an unmerged object.
180	
181	**3. Compound values never tokenise.** Chakra resolves a token only as the **entire** value.
182	`padding: 'xs 0'` is emitted verbatim and dropped by the browser. Use axis props
183	(`paddingInline`, `paddingBlock`).
184	
185	**4. A shorthand declared after a longhand resets it.** `padding: 0` after `paddingBlock`
186	wipes it. Order matters; prefer the axis props throughout.
187	
188	**5. `IconButton` hard-sets `padding: "0"`** as a style prop, merged *after* `__css`, so a `p:`
189	in your recipe size is discarded. **Size it with `minW`/`minH`** — which is also how you hit the
190	24×24 target-size requirement.
191	
192	**6. Register the recipe or destructuring throws at runtime.** Chakra resolves a recipe by the
193	string key passed to `useMultiStyleConfig`, not by file path — so co-location is free, but the
194	key must be in `theme/components/index.ts`.
195	
196	**7. Breakpoint tokens conflict with Chakra's.** `BP.desktop` is 64em; Chakra's `lg` is 62em
197	and `xl` is 80em. A responsive array silently steps at the wrong width. Write explicit media
198	queries:
199	
200	```ts
201	[`@media (min-width: ${BP.tablet})`]: { gap: 'var(--zimm-scale-3xl)' },
202	```
203	
204	The array shorthand also puts a bare token key at every step, and the guard flags all four.

208	## 3. Component structure
209	
210	### Placement — settled
211	
212	```
213	overrides/app/components/ui-kits/{atoms,molecules,organisms}/<camelCase>/index.tsx
214	```
215	
216	Being under `components/` is load-bearing for the registry generator, which scans that path.
217	
218	**Three casing families, each correct in its own context. Do not generalise between them:**
219	
220	| Family | Casing | Why |
221	|---|---|---|
222	| SFCC override | `product-tile/` kebab | must match upstream's import path |
223	| ui-kit component | `zimmButton/` camelCase | Zimmermann-authored — the default rule |
224	| `shared/ui` primitive | `Button/` PascalCase | mirrors upstream exactly |
225	
226	Kebab-case applies *only* to files mirroring a base Salesforce file. Note the theme key is
227	PascalCase (`ZimmTextInput`) while its recipe file is camelCase.
228	
229	### Tier is by composition, not visual size
230	
231	Read it off the imports, not the DOM:
232	
233	- **atom** — imports no other ui-kit. `zimmModal` is an atom despite being portal + backdrop +
234	  `role="dialog"` chrome, because it owns no content (`maxWidth`, `labelledBy`, children all
235	  come from the caller).
236	- **molecule** — composes atoms with light local logic. `zimmInputAction` = TextInput + Button
237	  + local validation state.
238	- **organism** — composes molecules/atoms **and owns domain state**. `zimmSubscribeSection`
239	  owns the subscribe state machine.
240	
241	An icon passed as a prop doesn't count (`icon="close"` keeps a Button an atom). Slotted
242	children don't count.
243	
244	**Storybook `title` is a different axis from the folder.** Folder = composition depth;
245	`title` = domain. `zimmModal` (atom) → `Elements/`; `zimmSubscribeSection` (organism) →
246	`Forms/`; `Footer` → `Layout/`. Don't conflate them.
247	
248	### Styling surface — a registered recipe, always
249	
250	Not inline styles, not a `.zimm-*` class, not a plain stylesheet. The recipe may live beside
251	the component as `<name>.css.ts` or centrally in `theme/components/` — Chakra resolves by
252	string key, so this is purely organisational.
253	
254	The argument against authoring in a stylesheet is worth keeping: a stylesheet can only see
255	`var(--zimm-*)`, which is **derived output at the bottom of the pipeline**. Author there and
256	you lose `textStyle`, the named `theme.space` scale, semantic colour tokens, and the theme
257	drift-guard tests. Not bad CSS — the wrong end of the pipeline.
258	
259	For a bespoke component wrapping a native element, the `chakra()` factory is the bridge:
260	native semantics plus recipe styling, read via `useMultiStyleConfig`.
261	
262	**Co-location changes who reviews it.** `CODEOWNERS:186`
263	(`overrides/app/components/**/*.css.ts` → squads only) is placed **last** among the
264	`components/` rules, and CODEOWNERS is last-match-wins, not most-specific-wins. So a `.css.ts`
265	inside `footer/` drops the Tier 2 approver requirement the surrounding directory carries,
266	while `footer/index.tsx` keeps it. The stated rationale: a co-located recipe *composes
267	established tokens*; authoring a new token still means `theme/foundation/` (Tier 1).
268	
269	`overrideStyling.md` flags its own inconsistency here rather than papering over it —
270	`zimmButton.css.ts` keys the app-wide `Button` recipe and is no longer designer-gated.
271	
272	### No data-fetching in `components/`
273	
274	Anything under `overrides/app/components/` receives data as props. Data-fetching belongs in
275	`overrides/app/pages/` or a container.
276	
277	**One documented exception:** Context-backed, app-wide static-content hooks (`useIntl`,
278	`useUiCopy`) may be called from any component including presentational leaves, because they
279	read from a Provider mounted above the route tree. Narrow by design — content identical for
280	every consumer regardless of route, not anything that varies per page.
281	
282	**Their no-Provider behaviour differs, and it matters for tests.** `useUiCopy` degrades:
283	`useContext(UiCopyContext) ?? FALLBACK_ONLY`, one line, renders with zero setup. **`useIntl`
284	throws** (`invariantIntlContext`), and its `IntlProvider` is mounted by the base SFCC `_app`,
285	not `_app-config` — a strictly narrower subtree. Any Vitest test rendering a `useIntl` consumer
286	must wrap it.
287	
288	### Two API patterns worth copying
289	
290	- **Encode the a11y contract in a discriminated union** so an inaccessible combination doesn't
291	  type-check.
292	- **Make an absent affordance opt-in**, not a silent default.
293	
294	### Do not trust the registry's tier column
295	
296	`generateRegistry.mjs:125-203` hardcodes tier arrays, lists no `ui-kits` path, and defaults
297	everything else to Tier 4. The registry is auto-generated and its *paths* are reliable; its
298	*tier* column is not.

322	## 4. What an override actually intercepts
323	
324	Three silent failure modes. In each, the override compiles, resolves, and never runs.
325	
326	**1. The resolver is webpack-only.** `ccExtensibility` in `package.json` redirects
327	`@salesforce/retail-react-app/...` imports to `overrides/` in the **real app build only**.
328	`.storybook/main.js` aliases that package straight to `node_modules`, and `vitest.config.ts`
329	doesn't touch it. So a base-path import of an already-overridden component builds correctly in
330	the shipped app and silently renders the **unstyled base version** in Storybook and Vitest —
331	the story looks like it's exercising your override and isn't.
332	
333	When importing a component that already has an override, use a **relative path**
334	(`'../swatch-group'`), not the base path.
335	
336	**2. A relative barrel re-export is not rewritten.** The attractive play — override
337	`shared/ui/<Name>` so branded styling propagates into base cart, checkout and account for free
338	— **does not work.** `shared/ui/index.jsx:29` does `export {Button} from './Button'`, a
339	relative export the resolver does not rewrite. And the consumption pattern is the wrong way
340	round: **212 base files import the barrel (195 excluding tests); 0 import `shared/ui/Button`.** The override
341	intercepts nothing.
342	
343	**3. A conditional render of an alternate module.** Overriding a component doesn't help if the
344	parent renders something else on that route. `footer` never reaches `/checkout`.
345	
346	**The generalised check**, before scoping any story around "override X and it propagates":
347	
348	```bash
349	grep -r "from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/<name>'" \
350	  node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/
351	```
352	
353	### The SFCC bridge pattern
354	
355	If a component is used internally by SFCC's own base components, its **default export must
356	stay a faithful, undecorated port** — full original prop surface, same `forwardRef` behaviour.
357	Put Zimmermann-only styling behind a **named export** that wraps it.
358	
359	⚠️ **No worked precedent exists in this repo.** `product-tile` is still base, `CardBaseline`
360	returns zero hits across `overrides/`, and `grep -rn forwardRef overrides/` returns one file.
361	Whoever needs this pattern first will be establishing it, not copying it.
362	
363	Where token-driven theming suffices, a theme recipe is preferable to a second export — the
364	prop-narrowing that motivated `CardBaseline` isn't needed for styling alone.

368	## 5. Figma to code
369	
370	### The discriminator is node type, not a fudge factor
371	
372	- **Text nodes** report a **cap-height box** (`text-box-trim: trim-both`,
373	  `text-box-edge: cap_alphabetic`). **Not comparable** to a CSS line box. Measured artifacts:
374	  "KEEP IN TOUCH" 8 vs 18, body copy 26 vs 36, `errorText` 9 vs 18.
375	- **Frames and instances** report a **real box**. **Directly comparable** — a delta here is a
376	  genuine defect. The `Textfield` *instance* at 44/59 against 45/68 was a real gap, and a naive
377	  "it's just cap height" rule would have wrongly dismissed it.
378	
379	**Supporting heuristic:** a *uniform* residual across siblings is measurement; a *varying* one
380	is a defect. Three contact items all sitting at +7 after every real cause was removed = the
381	heading's cap box.
382	
383	**Transfer the rule, not the numbers.** In shipped `zimmNavItem.css.ts`, deriving from
384	`lineHeight` + 4.5px padding produced 24/24/24/24/38 = 134 — exactly Figma's `Links` frame.
385	
386	### There are two Figma files and comparisons must be like-for-like
387	
388	`wPiWmZZOVKnrENUWk2XWWm` (design system) and `QQ427wHWEUjsjP7H8v48Rs` (composed page states).
389	Comparing an initial state from the design-system symbol against an error state from the page
390	file produced two wrong conclusions in a row — first "the slot is 59px in both states"
391	(actually `Subscribed=False` 320×44 vs `Subscribed=True` 308×59, with a compensating gap
392	change 40→24: the design **repositions**, it doesn't reserve), then a "reserve the slot" fix
393	that suppressed intended growth when the 68px padded box was already correct.
394	
395	### Frames are not breakpoints
396	
397	Frames exist at 402/1023/1440; breakpoint tokens are 768/860/1024. The unframed **768–1022
398	band was genuinely broken** — 18px horizontal scroll, 7 wrapped labels — and covers three iPad
399	models in portrait. `flexWrap: nowrap` prevents *breaking*, not *shrinking*: the row refused to
400	break, so the words broke instead.
401	
402	### Type metrics
403	
404	The fallback stack renders roughly **13% wider** than Futura Round, which is why serving the
405	real faces matters for parity review. `document.fonts.check()` returns `true` for unavailable
406	families and is useless — compare widths instead.
407	
408	### Measurement method
409	
410	**Subtract non-component bands before comparing totals** — the footer compares against 476,
411	not 606, once the `Disclaimer` band is excluded. **Isolate causes by cumulative in-DOM
412	mutation, one candidate at a time.** Measure `y` relative to the component root (Figma reports
413	frame-relative coordinates). Use
414	`domcontentloaded`, never `networkidle`, on a dev server. Dismiss the consent banner first.
415	`Range.getClientRects()` gives per-line widths to *prove* a wrap point. **Mutation-test layout
416	fixes at mobile** — two fixes read as Δ0 at 1440 only because a taller sibling column masked
417	them.
418	
419	**A design nudge is still spec.** Ship it and raise the question — don't silently "correct"
420	it, and don't silently ignore it. Document the deviation at the point of use.
421	
422	### No automated gate in this stack catches a layout defect
423	
424	`width: 'xl'` resolving to 576px destroyed the footer on every page while passing `tsc`,
425	`eslint`, `vitest`, local *and* remote CodeRabbit, and the Storybook a11y run. Only rendering
426	beside Figma found it.

430	## 6. Layout mechanics
431	
432	Six mechanisms, each with the fix that actually worked.
433	
434	1. **A wrapped element takes available width, not its longest line.** `width: min-content`
435	   resolves to the widest unbreakable run — usually what you want when a column should hug its
436	   longest word rather than its container.
437	
438	2. **`minHeight` plus `align-items: center` loses leading when content wraps.** The centring
439	   discards the extra line's leading rather than growing the box. Derive height from
440	   `lineHeight` plus padding instead of reserving a `minHeight`.
441	
442	3. **An inline child inside a block parent leaks descender space.** A block-level `<li>`
443	   wrapping an `inline-flex` `<a>` gets a line box whose strut sits below the baseline —
444	   measured **25.5px against the anchor's own 24px**, leaking 1.5px per row (3px on a wrapped
445	   label) and making the footer's links column 9px taller than Figma's 158px.
446	   **Fix: `display: flex` on the `<li>`**, which removes the line box entirely.
447	   `footerNavColumn.css.ts:69` is the shipped instance.
448	   ⚠️ `display: block` is the **bug**, not the fix.
449	
450	4. **Give the gap to the heading, not the column.** If the design nests a group inside a stack
451	   with no gap, don't reproduce it as a sibling in a gapped flex container — the container's
452	   gap then applies where the design has none. Put the spacing on the heading's `marginBottom`.
453	
454	5. **`flexWrap: nowrap` prevents breaking, not shrinking.** The row refuses to break, so the
455	   words break instead. This is what broke the unframed 768–1022 band.
456	
457	6. **A non-breaking space must be the `\u00A0` escape**, not a literal character in source —
458	   invisible to review and unpredictable under reformatting. Note the dependency it creates:
459	   production copy has to carry the same character.
460	
461	**A solution window measured in single pixels is a coincidence, not a tolerance.** The footer's
462	viable column cap was **[131, 132.9) — 1.9px wide**. Treat that as a signal the constraint set
463	is over-determined, not as a fix that happens to work.
464	
465	## 7. Building against absent data
466	
467	### Three patterns, only the first correct
468	
469	**Guard, then render inert but perceivable.** Never render nothing where a control was
470	promised; never render a control that can't act.
471	
472	- **An empty-string fallback is a layout bug** — `heading ?? ''` renders an empty element that
473	  **keeps its margins**, measured as a roughly 64px void. It doesn't collapse; it reserves
474	  space for nothing.
475	- **A silent element swap actively lies** — it promises an affordance that isn't there.
476	- **Fix at the atom**, not at each call site.
477	
478	### The three-tier policy — the most reusable decision in the footer build
479	
480	Behaviour differs by what the content *is*:
481	
482	| Content class | Behaviour | Why |
483	|---|---|---|
484	| **Structural** (`footerConfig`) | render **nothing** — `if (!footerData) return null` | no fallback to placeholder once wired to live data, so an outage doesn't ship stale placeholder copy to real shoppers |
485	| **Microcopy** (`uiCopy`) | fall back to the **English literal** | losing a button label to an outage should never blank a control |
486	| **Per-item destination** (a contact href) | degrade **that item only** to a labelled non-interactive `<span>` | perceivable, but no false affordance |
487	
488	The per-item case is the carefully argued one: no `href`, no `tabIndex`, so nothing promises an
489	action that cannot be performed (WCAG 2.4.4 / 3.2.4) — but **labelled, not `aria-hidden`**, so
490	a screen-reader user learns the channel exists instead of getting silence (avoiding the 1.1.1
491	information loss an earlier `aria-hidden` caused).
492	
493	The same treatment is reused three times for "control with no action": the contact fallback,
494	`ZimmNavItem`'s no-href branch (renders a `<button>` that doesn't navigate), and `BottomBar`'s
495	locale placeholder (a `<div>`, deliberately not a `<button>`).
496	
497	### Never branch on localised CMS text
498	
499	`footerNavGroup` carries `showContactChannels: boolean` rather than matching
500	`heading === 'Contact'` — because `heading` is localised and silently stops matching the moment
501	an editor writes "Kontakt" or "Contacto". This footer ships to eight storefronts.
502	
503	### Guarding hrefs
504	
505	Every CMS-sourced href passes `isSafeHref` before reaching an anchor. The subtlety: WHATWG URL
506	parsing strips C0 control characters, tab, LF and CR *before* scheme detection, so a naive
507	`^javascript:` regex is bypassed by `java\tscript:`. **Normalise, then test.**
508

511	## 8. CMS data and the tier reality
512	
513	New section. The footer rendered correctly in dev and was blank on the test tier, and nothing
514	in the component was wrong.
515	
516	### Content types and entries promote by different mechanisms
517	
518	| | Content **types** (schema) | Content (**entries**) |
519	|---|---|---|
520	| Mechanism | org-scoped Environment Template | *nothing automated* |
521	| Build | `npm run sync:contentful` | — |
522	| Deploy | `npm run install:contentful -- --target <env>` | — |
523	
524	**A template cannot carry entries — this is structural.** The SDK type has exactly two slots:
525	
526	```ts
527	// contentful-management/dist/types/entities/environment-template.d.ts:31-34
528	entities: {
529	    contentTypeTemplates: Array<ContentTypeTemplateProps>;
530	    editorInterfaceTemplates: Array<EditorInterfaceTemplateProps>;
531	};
532	```
533	
534	No `entries`, no `assets`. The only entry-writing code in the repo is `seedRegions.mjs:71-72`,
535	which handles the 11 `region` entries and nothing else.
536	
537	### Verified tier state, 2026-08-25
538	
539	| tier | content types | published entries |
540	|---|---|---|
541	| **dev** | **14** | **42** (+3 assets) |
542	| test / sit / uat / staging | **0** | **0** |
543	| prod | no environment id configured | — |
544	
545	The environments exist — the CDA returned `total: 0`, not `NotFound`. Nothing has ever been
546	promoted out of dev.
547	
548	**The template covers 5 of dev's 14 types** — `footerConfig`, `footerNavGroup`, `link`,
549	`region`, `uiCopy`. The other 9 exist only inside the dev environment, UI-authored, with no
550	code representation, and `install:contentful` cannot move them.
551	
552	**There is no forward content promotion in this repo at all.** The actual release model is the
553	alias flip in `promoteAlias.mjs`: clone master → install template → author and verify →
554	repoint `production`/`master`. Content moves *backwards* (master → clone), never forwards.

557	
558	`include: 3` is not arbitrary. At depth 2 the `regions` array arrives as unresolved stubs,
559	`region.fields.siteId` throws, the `.catch` swallows it, and the **entire footer renders
560	nothing**. A resolution-depth mistake looks identical to a network failure from the page.

562	### Locale is not passed on any Contentful fetch
563	
564	`useContentful.ts:110` builds a URL with `content_type`, `access_token` and `include` only, so
565	the footer and `uiCopy` get the space default on all eight storefronts. Three invocation sites
566	across two production files. (`pages/experience/` and `pages/contentfulPreview/` *do* pass

568	hook signature change, which is a team RFC.

571	
572	```bash
573	curl -s "https://cdn.contentful.com/spaces/<space>/environments/<env>/entries?content_type=<type>&limit=1" \
574	  -H "Authorization: Bearer <that tier's delivery token>"
575	```

577	`total: 1` means it will render. `unknownContentType` means the model was never installed.
578	Note the CDA returns an unreliable `total` at `limit=0` — use `limit=1`.

582	## 9. Accessibility patterns
583	
584	Six recurring success criteria and what each actually demanded.
585	
586	- **1.1.1** — a degraded control must stay *labelled*, not `aria-hidden`. Silence is
587	  information loss.
588	- **1.4.4 / 1.4.10** — `rem` for anything that must survive zoom; a modal panel needs
589	  `maxHeight` + `overflowY` or tall content centres half-off-screen and is unreachable.
590	- **2.4.4 / 3.2.4** — no `href` and no `tabIndex` on a control that cannot act, so nothing
591	  promises an action that can't be performed.
592	- **2.5.8** — 24×24 minimum target size, which is a WCAG **2.2** addition and easy to miss if
593	  working from a 2.1 checklist.
594	- **2.5.3 Label in name** — the accessible name must *contain* the visible label.
595	- **3.2.5** — a link leaving the site gets `rel="noopener noreferrer"` and a suffix in its
596	  accessible name. That is the project's external-link standard; it lives nowhere else.
597	- **Focus** — a programmatic `.focus()` does **not** match `:focus-visible`. A focus ring
598	  styled only on `:focus-visible` will not appear after a scripted focus move.
599	- **Portal + focus trap** — when `activeElement` is outside the trap, the trap must handle it
600	  rather than assume containment.
601	
602	Every `IconButton` needs `aria-label`; every `<img>` needs `alt` (`alt=""` for decorative).
603	Note the ast-grep rule matches `^img$` only, so Chakra's `<Image>` is invisible to it, and its
604	`aria-label` check does not match `aria-labelledby`.

608	## 10. Verification: what actually proves anything
609	
610	### The integrity principle
611	
612	> The verification instrument was built from the same belief as the thing it verified, and was
613	> never made to fail on purpose.
614	
615	That is the single recurring failure mode. A green check that was never proven capable of going
616	red carries no information.
617	
618	Catalogued instances, all self-caught after reporting a false all-clear: a `safeHref` suite
619	reported "well covered, 3 layers" whose 13 cases contained **zero backslashes** — the exact
620	vector already named; a `fontFace` test iterating an empty array; a mutation test that
621	"passed" because `perl -pi` works line-at-a-time and cannot match `\n`; a recipe parity check
622	that false-alarmed three times on recipes whose `baseStyle` is a **function**; a literal-count
623	sweep that inflated 19→41 by matching `.rem` inside `removeEventListener`.
624	
625	### Copy the non-vacuity meta-test
626	
627	`recipeGuards.test.ts` includes `test('collect() actually walks the registered recipes')`
628	precisely because every other guard asserts `toEqual([])`, which an empty input satisfies.
629	Stubbing `components` to `{}` turned the whole file green — verified.
630	
631	Same shape for layout assertions: a pure before/after equality is satisfied vacuously by a
632	collapsed container (`display:none`, `height:0`, an ancestor `display:none` — and every rect
633	is 0 in jsdom). **Anchor the measurement above zero first.**
634	
635	And resolve a function-form `baseStyle` across **all** boolean prop combinations, not the
636	default one. The original bug hid down a conditional branch a single-resolution walk never
637	entered.
638	
639	### Green tests that encode the bug
640	
641	A suite can test *around* a defect. The region tie-break suite had a case named "order of the
642	tied candidates does not change the outcome" that used only **distinct** timestamps — the one
643	arrangement already order-independent. It passed while the bug was live.
644	
645	Mutation testing is necessary but not sufficient: it proves the check *can* fail, not that it
646	fails for the right reason.
647	
648	### [CORRECTED] What is and is not gated
649	
650	**a11y IS gated.** An earlier belief — repeated four times in one session and again by a fresh
651	analysis this week — was that a11y is ungated because there is no `.storybook/test-runner.js`.
652	**That is Storybook 8 knowledge and is wrong for what is installed.**
653	`@storybook/test-runner@0.24.4`'s `dist/setup-page-script.js:390-397` reads
654	`story.parameters?.a11y?.test` and throws when it `=== "error"`; `.storybook/preview.tsx:44`
655	sets exactly that. No `test-runner.js` is needed. **Do not delete that `preview.tsx` block.**
656	
657	Honest rider: the gate has never been made to fail on purpose, so by the standard above it is
658	**unproven, not absent**.
659	
660	**Gated nowhere at all:** `eslint`, `prettier`, `tsc --noEmit`, `audit:tokens`, any CSS bundle
661	budget, test coverage. `npm run lint` currently fails repo-wide on pre-existing prettier errors
662	and CI never notices.
663	
664	**A skipped required check counts as passing.** Live on PR #59: all four suites reported
665	`skipping` — including both *required* checks — while `mergeable: true`. `detect-changes` uses
666	`since_last_remote_commit`, and a final push touching only registry files fell outside every
667	allow-list. A 93-commit PR became merge-eligible with **zero test evidence on its head SHA**.
668	Read `gh pr checks` for `skipping`, not just for green.
669	
670	**A named gate that cannot fail:** `npm run test:contracts` is `echo 'TODO…' && exit 0`, and
671	it is a hard `needs` of `sit-gate`.
672	
673	### Harness traps
674	
675	- **`test-storybook` needs a *built* Storybook.** Dev-server runs made four mutation results
676	  uninterpretable.
677	- **Vitest does not run `play`.**
678	- **jsdom always provides `window`**, so an SSR branch needs `// @vitest-environment node`.
679	- **Every jsdom rect is 0** — layout assertions there are meaningless.
680	- **`ZimmIcon` throws under Vitest.** It imports the base SFCC icons barrel, whose top-level
681	  `AmexSymbol.viewBox = ...` fails because SVG imports resolve to raw path strings here.
682	  Unfixable from a test file (`vitest.config.ts` is Tier 1). Mock at the smallest surface:
683	  ```ts
684	  vi.mock('app/components/ui-kits/atoms/zimmIcon', () => ({ ZimmIcon: () => null }))
685	  ```
686	  …or forward `aria-label`/`aria-hidden` when an assertion depends on the accessible name.
687	- **Portalled content is scoped to `document.body`, not `canvasElement`.** `canvasElement` is
688	  `#storybook-root`, a *sibling* of the portal target. Measured: `canvasElement.innerHTML` is
689	  41 characters, 0 dialogs inside the canvas against 1 in the document. A canvas-scoped
690	  `getByRole` fails immediately; `findByRole` fails after ~1002ms; the body-scoped form passes
691	  in 1–2ms. `testing.md:128`'s "never reach into `document`" has no portal carve-out — that is
692	  a documentation defect, not a code one.
693	- **`@storybook/test` is not installed.** `testing.md:115` prescribes it; Storybook 10 moved it
694	  to `storybook/test`. Following that line verbatim breaks.
695	
696	### The gap no tool covers
697	
698	Duplication and reuse. No tool detects "this is a second Button." Nothing catches a bare token
699	key used as a JSX prop. Nothing catches a layout defect. Nothing catches a component whose data
700	doesn't exist on the tier it ships to.
701	
702	---
703	
704	## 11. Signposts in the repo that point at nothing
705	
706	Each of these has already cost time.
707	
708	- **`overrides.md` does not exist.** `overrideStyling.md:4,112,179` references it three times
709	  and positions it as the companion doc defining module-replacement correctness. It exists only
710	  on two unmerged spike branches.
711	- **`overrideStyling.md` is orphaned and unsynced.** `AGENTS.md` never references it
712	  (`grep -c` → 0). `scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs`'s manifest omits it, along with `css.md`,
713	  `components.md`, `typescript.md` and `tagging.md` — three of which are in `conventions.md`'s
714	  own "See also" list. The largest rules file, holding the entire styling hierarchy, is
715	  invisible to Cursor and Copilot.
716	- **The rules set is split on its own component convention.** `components.md` and
717	  `conventions.md` contain **zero** occurrences of `ui-kits`, `atoms`, `molecules` or
718	  `organisms`. `new-component/SKILL.md:29` still scaffolds to the flat path.
719	  `.docs/architecture.md` contradicts itself — `:136` cites the correct
720	  `ui-kits/atoms/zimmButton/zimmButton.css.ts` while `:130`/`:139` prescribe a
721	  `components/custom/` directory that has never existed.
722	- **[CORRECTED] `scripts/auditTokenUsage.mjs` now exists.** Earlier notes said it didn't. It
723	  was built 2026-08-23 and `npm run audit:tokens` is wired. It is still **not in CI** — a
724	  current run reports **19 unacknowledged violations**, 14 pre-existing plus 5 in
725	  `product-view/index.tsx`.
726	- **`test:lighthouse` is broken.** `package.json:57` points at `tests/lighthouserc.js`; the
727	  real file is `./lighthouserc.js` and there is no `tests/` directory. CI is unaffected —
728	  `digital-sit.yml` runs bare `lhci autorun`, which auto-discovers. `AGENTS.md:37` names the
729	  same dead path.
730	- **`deploy-dev.yml`'s `tag-sprint` job reads `scripts/sprint.txt`**, which does not exist and
731	  never has. The job runs on every dev deploy and is a guarded permanent no-op — no sprint tag
732	  has ever been created.
733	- **`squadA.md` and `squadB.md` are largely fiction.** Of squadA's 21 territory paths, 4 exist;
734	  **zero** of squadB's 9 do. Both instruct edits to files not in the repo, and both were last
735	  touched 2026-07-14. And they contradict `CODEOWNERS` on PDP ownership —
736	  CODEOWNERS says Squad B and is the one that enforces.
737	- **`sprintScope.md` is two months stale** and `AGENTS.md` Hard Rule 14 makes it load-bearing
738	  for scoping. It says "Sprint 0 — Foundation (in progress)" while its own table puts today in
739	  Sprint 5. Applied literally it would classify current PDP work as past-sprint.
740	- **`.docs/architecture.md` misstates the stack**: React Router v6 (actually 5.3.4 — the
741	  footer uses `useHistory`), Storybook 8 (actually 10.4.6), axe via `vitest-axe`/`axe-playwright`
742	  (neither installed), Playwright "not yet configured" (7 projects, two workflows), "all
743	  services mocked (MSW stubs)" — `msw@1.3.5` is present transitively but has zero references in
744	  `overrides/`, and it is a test tool, not a local-dev data source. (`AGENTS.md` bans MSW in
745	  *production paths* only; `testing.md` permits it for integration tests.)
746	- **`CONTENT_TYPE_IDS`** (`overrides/app/config/contentfulMapping.ts:53` — note the top-level
747	  `config/` is a different, Tier 1 directory) has zero consumers and duplicates
748	  `scripts/contentful/content-types/*.js`.
749	- **`connectionPools.ts` looks like live infrastructure and is dead code** — `ssr.js` doesn't
750	  import it. The blast-radius isolation its header claims is not in effect.
751	
752	**The pattern:** trust the code, `CODEOWNERS`, `recipeGuards.test.ts`, and `tagging.md`.
753	Verify everything else before citing it. A rules file's worked example is as likely to describe
754	an unmerged branch as the one you're on.
755	
756	---
757	
758	*Compiled 2026-08-25 from the SFCC-55 global-footer build (PR #59, 93 commits, merged
759	2026-08-24) and the Contentful tier investigation that followed it. Claims re-measured against
